title: Agenda
text: Buckingham County Planning Commission Work Session Agenda Monday, November 16, 2026 6:00PM Buckingham County Administration Building Peter Francisco Meeting Room 1. Call to Order by Planning Commission Chairman Invocation Pledge of Allegiance Establishment of Quorums 2. Adoption of Agenda 3. Discussion Topic a. Technology Overlay 4. Commission Matters and Concerns 5. Adjournment BUCKINGHAM COUNTY • PLANNING COMMISSION Building Standards Into a Technology Overlay District How the county sets the rules — and what those rules are Staff discussion document — Nici Edmondston • E. M. Wright, Jr. Zoning lets us direct where growth goes The purpose behind an overlay The county can’t turn off demand for data centers and energy projects — but zoning lets us decide where they go, and on what terms. Channel intensive uses Protect what’s rural Direct data centers, advanced manufacturing, and energy projects to land already industrial in character — where transmission, water, and roads already exist. Relieve the pressure that would otherwise push these uses onto working farmland and open countryside — keeping the rest of the county rural. The overlay is a means of protecting the county’s rural heritage — keeping industry where industry has always been. Direct development to where it fits Concentrate intensive uses on suitable land; keep the countryside rural BRING APPROPRIATE DEVELOPMENT HERE KEEP THIS RURAL • Land already industrial — or long used for mining and quarrying • Working farmland and forestland • On or near high-voltage transmission • Adequate water and road capacity • Separated from homes and schools • Open countryside and scenic corridors • Residential communities • Rural roads and small-town character Concentrating intensive uses where they already belong relieves the pressure to convert farmland — protecting rural character, not diminishing it. Why this is on the agenda The starting conditions shape everything that follows By right, but scarce No standards No applications Data centers are a by-right use in M-1 and M-2 — but those districts barely exist on the ground, so many projects would arrive by rezoning. Nothing in the ordinance governs their noise, height, setbacks, buffers, water use, or decommissioning. Nothing is pending or approved. A clean slate to set the rules first — no vesting, no pressure. The task: put standards in place before a project arrives — ready for both paths, by-right use of existing M-1/M-2 and the rezonings that create new industrial land. What the zoning map already shows The county has a map — of districts. Industrial land is scarce. Districts that matter tonight A-1 Agricultural A-1 with SUP granted B-1 Business R-1 Residential M-1 / M-2 Industrial Town of Dillwyn A-1 is the county. Nearly every acre is Agricultural; the other districts are small islands. That is why the special use permit, not the district, is where most land-use decisions get made. Industrial land is scarce. M-1 and M-2 appear in only a handful of patches. A data center’s by-right entry point barely exists on the ground — so the rezoning that creates industrial land is often the real decision. The gold patches are the record. Source: Buckingham County Zoning Map (interactiveGIS), printed 08/21/2026. Each is a special use permit already granted in A-1. Opposition hasn’t stopped projects — the Commission has been approving them one at a time. What an overlay is A second layer of rules on top of the base zoning Every parcel already has a base zoning district (A-1, M-1, M-2, R-1). An overlay adds a second layer of rules inside a mapped boundary. OVERLAY added uses + standards • The base zoning does not go away. • Inside the line, the overlay adds or tightens uses and standards. • Outside the line, the overlay does not exist and changes nothing. BASE ZONING — M-1 / M-2 The overlay sits on top of the base zoning, within the boundary. Where the standards actually live “By right” does not mean “no conditions” — it changes when and where they are set By-right uses Special Use Permit uses • Conditions are written into the ordinance in advance, as objective standards. • Conditions are set case by case, at a public hearing. • Staff review is administrative: check the project against the standards — approve if it complies. • No project-by-project negotiation, and proffers are not available. • The ordinance IS the policy. • The Board can attach tailored conditions or deny. • Maximum discretion on each project — less predictability for applicants. • Best reserved for the highest-impact uses. For anything by right, whatever the county wants to require must be anticipated and written down now. A key choice for the Commission How each allowed use is permitted A By right + SUP for the highest-impact uses B All uses by right under uniform standards • Ordinary tech uses by right under standards. • Every use by right if it meets the written standards. • Generating stations, SMRs, off-site export → Special Use Permit. • Control lives in rigorous, uniform rules — no special-use step. • Keeps case-by-case control over the biggest projects. • Maximum predictability; scrutiny front-loaded into the ordinance. • Trade-off: less predictability. • Trade-off: no per-project hearing. Many ordinances mix the two, using size/capacity thresholds to decide which lane a use falls in. The case for “by right” Control through clear standards set in advance — not case-by-case discretion 1 Predictability attracts investment Defined uses and standards draw bettercapitalized, higher-quality applicants and shorten the path to a decision. 4 Faster, lower-cost review Compliant projects are approved administratively — no repeated hearings for each application. 2 Set once, in daylight Terms are debated and adopted publicly, up front — not negotiated project by project under deadline pressure. 5 Protections are concrete Because everything must be written down first, safeguards are specific and enforceable — not left to negotiation. 3 Applied equally to all Objective standards every project must meet; no ad hoc deals, and a lower risk of legal challenge. 6 Leverage stays with the county The county sets the terms before any applicant is at the table — strongest while nothing is pending. By right and SUP are not all-or-nothing: the county can still route the highest-impact uses to a Special Use Permit using capacity thresholds. When a Special Use Permit fits better Case-by-case control for the highest-impact uses 1 Case-by-case scrutiny Each major project is judged on its own facts, its own site, and its actual impacts. 4 Authority to deny The Board can say no to a project that is wrong for the spot, even if it meets the standards. 2 Tailored conditions The Board can attach project-specific conditions a uniform standard could never anticipate. 5 Fits novel or uncertain uses Best where impacts aren’t yet well understood — merchant generation, SMRs — and good standards can’t be written yet. 3 A public hearing on each Neighbors get a formal voice on every high-impact project — not only at the ordinance stage. 6 Discretion stays with the Board Elected officials keep the final call on the county’s biggest land-use decisions. The trade-off is less predictability and more process — so SUP is best reserved for the highest-impact uses, not routine ones. What the standards are The parameters written into the ordinance and applied to every project 1 Noise Decibel limits at residential property lines; third-party modeling before and after. 5 Water & infrastructure Demonstrated water, sewer, and road capacity before approval. 2 Height & setbacks Building height caps and large setbacks, especially from homes. 6 Construction & traffic Limited construction hours; traffic management. 3 Buffers & screening Vegetated buffers and screening to keep facilities out of sight. 7 Master-plan review Whole-site plan approved before any building permit issues. 4 Lighting Full cut-off / dark-sky limits on light spillover. 8 Decommissioning Removal obligations plus a bond or financial assurance. Standards are needed either way The by-right status in M-1 and M-2 makes this true with or without an overlay Data centers are already permitted by right in M-1 and M-2 — though those districts are scarce, so many projects would arrive by rezoning. Either path lands in an industrial district with no use-specific rules today, so developing standards stands on its own, independent of the overlay decision. If an overlay IS adopted If an overlay is NOT adopted It governs only the mapped area. M-1/M-2 land outside the boundary stays by right with no standards — the gap remains. The base districts are the only place rules can live. With no standards, there is no protection anywhere the use is allowed. Either way: the baseline standards apply automatically to by-right uses across all of M-1 and M-2 — self-executing, with no permit or hearing needed to trigger them. Any Special Use Permit the overlay uses for the highest-impact uses is a separate layer on top; it does not replace or gate these base standards. The priority: adopt standards quickly Attach enforceable standards to the by-right uses now — without changing their by-right status 1 Adopt baseline standards now • Add enforceable performance standards to M-1 / M-2 by a focused text amendment. • The uses stay by right — projects simply must meet the written rules. • Fast protection that applies wherever the districts exist. 2 Continue the overlay in parallel • Tailored, enhanced standards and added energy uses for a chosen area. • On its own deliberate, multi-session timeline. • Builds on the baseline — it does not replace or gate it. The goal is speed and protection: get enforceable standards on the books now. This adds rules to the by-right uses — it does not remove them or route them to a Special Use Permit. The sequence How the Commission moves from interest to adoption • Start with the gate: does the Commission want to pursue it? • Develop drafts and options with staff — over several work sessions. • Set siting criteria, the area, and the use list. • Decide how each use is permitted — by right vs. Special Use Permit — then write the criteria and conditions. • Confirm Comp Plan fit, engage the public, then hearings and recommendation. What staff is asking No vote on an ordinance or a site today 1 Receive this introduction Get a common footing on overlays and how standards are built in. 2 Discuss the key choice Weigh by-right vs. Special Use Permit, and the base-vs-overlay tracks. 3 Direct staff to develop drafts & options Bring alternatives back for the full Commission — not a finished draft. 4 Set expectations Plan for several work sessions before any public hearing. Set the rules first — on the county’s terms. Standards adopted in daylight, before any project arrives, protect residents and keep control with the county. Discussion

The purpose of this amendment is to clarify that only the amount of a non-discretionary gratuity that exceeds 20% of the purchase price is subject to food & beverage taxes in accordance with the Code of Virginia. Chapter 103 ARTICLE IX - Exemption for Elderly and Disabled Persons. (Real Estate). The purpose of this amendment is to reduce the qualifying acreage for the County’s real estate tax relief program for qualifying elderly & handicapped from 10 acres to 1 acre. In conjunction with the reduction in qualifying acreage, the annual household income and net worth thresholds used to calculate the percentage of the exemption and total tax exemption are proposed to increase. Chapter 103 ARTICLE VII – Transient Occupancy Tax. The purpose of this amendment is to incorporate changes to state law enacted by the General Assembly in the Code of Caroline County. The changes require accommodations intermediaries (i.e. Airbnb, Expedia, VRBO, etc.) to submit monthly a list of property addresses and gross receipts of all bookings made within each locality and requires accommodation providers (i.e. the homeowner providing the accommodations) that solely use an accommodations intermediary to book accommodations to file an annual attestation to that fact in order to be exempt from filing monthly transient occupancy remittances. Action on Comprehensive Plan Modernization "PlanMod" Amendment 26PJ0006 Chesterfield County Planning Commission Meeting November 17, 2026 PlanMod is an amendment to Moving Forward - The Comprehensive Plan for Chesterfield. Virginia law requires that all local governments adopt, and periodically update, their comprehensive plan. The Plan does not rezone property or change uses or densities of property. The amendment includes updates and revisions to language, data, charts, tables, maps and graphics throughout the entire Plan, including but not limited to updates to the Land Use Plan and Thoroughfare Plan maps. Some of the chapters of the Plan have been renamed or renumbered. The proposed draft Land Use Plan Map reflects how the county is growing and changing to better align with existing development patterns, current market conditions, and the natural character of different parts of the county. Generally, the proposed changes to the Land Use Plan map include: lowering residential densities south and west of Route 288; reducing areas designated with the mixed-use categories; reducing areas designated with Office, Light Production & Assembly; and updating the Conservation/Recreation and Institutional designations to meet the new criteria outlined within these categories. The Land Use Plan serves as guide for zoning, land use and development decisions, but does not rezone or regulate property. The Planning Commission held a public hearing on October 20, 2026, on the Comprehensive Plan Amendment - Comprehensive Plan Modernization "PlanMod", and after taking public comment, closed the public hearing. Action on the Comprehensive Plan Amendment for the Comprehensive Plan Modernization "PlanMod" was deferred until the November 17, 2026, Planning Commission meeting. 16. The meeting may also be viewed on the City's streaming platforms and local government Channel 10. Individuals with disabilities who require assistance or special arrangements to participate in the public meeting may call (434) 987-1267 or submit a request via email to ada@charlottesville.gov. The City of Charlottesville requests that you provide 48 hours’ notice so that proper arrangements may be made. • The presiding officer shall ensure that individuals address their comments to City Council at appropriate times, in accordance with the meeting agenda and Council’s Rules of Procedure. • No person who is not a member of the city council shall orally address it until leave to do so has been granted by the city council or until invited to do so by the mayor. (City Code sec.2-71) • Remarks and actions that disrupt the progress of the Council meeting, and remarks from persons other than councilors, the City Manager, the City Attorney, or a presenter for an Agenda Item are not permitted. • The presiding officer shall call an individual to order, including a councilor, when that individual goes afoul of these rules. The following are examples of remarks and behavior that are not permitted: • i. Interrupting a speaker who is addressing Council at the speaker's microphone, or interrupting a speaker who has otherwise been invited to address Council during Community Matters or a Public Hearing ii. Interrupting a councilor who is speaking iii. Shouting, and talking (either individually or in concert with others) in a manner that prevents a speaker or a Councilor from being heard or that otherwise hinders the progress of the meeting iv. Blocking paths for emergency exit from the meeting room; engaging in any conduct that prevents a member of the audience from seeing or hearing councilors during a meeting; standing on chairs or tables within the Council meeting room v. Threats or incitement of violence toward councilors, City staff or members of the public vi. Engaging in conduct that is a criminal offense under the City Code or the Virginia Code vii. Campaigning for elected office viii. Promotion of private business ventures ix. Using profanity or vulgarity x. Personal attacks against Councilors, City staff or members of the public xi. Behavior which tends to intimidate others During a City Council meeting the presiding officer shall have control of the Council Chambers and the connecting halls and corridors within City Hall, and any other venue where a Council meeting is being held. In case of any conduct described above, the presiding officer may take measures deemed appropriate, including but not limited to suspending the meeting until order is restored, ordering areas to be cleared by the Sergeant at Arms, or requiring any individual to exit the meeting room and adjacent premises (connecting halls and corridors.)

title: Call for Applicants for the Covington Redevelopment & Housing Authority - Released 11/02/2026
text: CITY OF COVINGTON CALL FOR APPLICANTS COVINGTON HOUSING AUTHORITY SEAT VACANCY NOTICE DATE: Friday, November 6, 2026 The City of Covington Council is accepting applications from qualified individuals interested in serving on the Covington Redevelopment and Housing Authority. Applicants must meet the applicable residency requirements for Housing Authority commissioners and must reside within the City of Covington city limits, which is the Authority’s area of operation. This residency requirement is based on Title 36 of the Code of Virginia, §36-18. The Housing Authority plays an important role in supporting housing programs, redevelopment efforts, and related community initiatives within the City. Applicants must submit: • A letter of interest; and • A current resume. Applications will be accepted until the vacant seat is filled. Qualified applicants will be notified of the City Council meeting at which the appointment will be considered and will be asked to attend in case Council would like to speak with them before making the appointment. Please submit materials to: Amber N. Berberette City Clerk to Council City of Covington 333 W. Locust Street Covington, VA 24426 Phone: (540) 965-6302 Email: cityclerk@covington.va.us Applications will be reviewed by City Council for consideration and appointment. For reference, VA Code §36-18: https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title36/chapter1/section36-18/ PAGE 1 OF 1

text: MARTINSVILLE CITY COUNCIL MEETING AGENDA Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Martinsville’s Vision Martinsville is a thriving, full-service city centrally located in southern Virginia, offering excellent education and superior quality of life in a picturesque setting while embracing inclusivity and opportunities to ensure a sustainable and fulfilling lifestyle to live, visit, and grow. Martinsville’s Mission Martinsville City proudly promotes a safe, healthy, thriving community dedicated to delivering excellent services and meaningful public participation. News & Events Communications from Visitors / Business from the Floor Description: The purpose of City Council Meetings is to conduct the City’s Business. City Council allows for public comment, limited to matters on which the Council has the power and authority to act and are not listed on the printed agenda. Participation: Citizens who wish to participate in a meeting’s public comment period may do so by signing up at the podium at the entrance prior to the beginning of the meeting, emailing their comments to Peyton Nibblett, Deputy City Clerk, at pnibblett@martinsvilleva.gov, calling in their comments to 276-403-5196, or mailing comments to the City of Martinsville, attn.: Peyton Nibblett, Martinsville, VA 24114 (a.) Comments, or a request to speak, must be received by noon the day before a Council meeting for consideration by the Council at the meeting. (b.) Any person submitting comments or requesting to speak must identify themselves by name and address, including zip code. (c.) Remarks are to be limited to 3 minutes or less (as read aloud),address a topic of City business, and refrain from making any personal references or accusations of a factually false and/or malicious nature. (d.) Priority for comments is given to City residents, taxpayers, and business owners.(e.) Speakers may not yield time. (f.) Groups of speakers on the same topic must designate a single representative. Comments violating these rules may not be presented at the Council meeting. (g.) Any speaker violating these rules may be removed from the podium or from the Council Chamber. (h.) text: City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL INFORMAL SESSION November 2, 2026 9:00 AM City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW AGENDA The City of Roanoke is a safe, caring and economically vibrant community in which to live, learn, work, play and prosper. A vibrant urban center with strong neighborhoods set amongst the spectacular beauty of Virginia's Blue Ridge. NOTICE: City Council meetings will be televised live and replayed on RVTV Channel 3 on Thursdays at 7:00 pm, and Saturdays from 10:00 am to 5:00 pm; and video streamed through YouTube Live at youtube.com/RoanokeVa. Council meetings are offered with closed captioning for the deaf or hard of hearing. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. Welcome ITEMS FOR ACTION: A communication from Mayor Joseph L. Cobb requesting that the Council convene in a Closed Meeting to discuss vacancies on certain authorities, boards, commissions and committees appointed by the Council, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(1), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. (7-0) A communication from Mayor Joseph L. Cobb requesting that Council convene in a Closed Meeting to discuss the 2026 Citizen of the Year Award, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(10), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. (7-0) A communication from the City Attorney requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting to consult with legal counsel pertaining to actual litigation regarding a status update, where such consultation or briefing in open meeting would adversely affect the negotiating or litigating posture of the public body, pursuant to Section 2.23711 (A)(7), Code of Virginia. (7-0) A communication from the City Attorney requesting that Council convene in a closed meeting to consult with legal counsel regarding a certain legal matter requiring the provision of legal advice by outside counsel involving an internal investigation, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(8), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. (7-0) Items listed on the 2:00 pm City Council docket requiring discussion/clarification and addition/deletions to the 2:00 pm agenda. None. Topics for discussion by the Mayor and Members of City Council. None. BRIEFING: Western Virginia Water Authority - Water Supply Study Results - 30 minutes LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE MEETING SCHEDULED FOR 9:00 am, IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER. (9:08 am - 10:10 am) AT 11:21 AM, THE COUNCIL MEETING WAS DECLARED IN RECESS FOR A CLOSED MEETING; AND THEREAFTER RECONVENE AT 2:00 pm, IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER, ROOM 450, NOEL C. TAYLOR MUNICIPAL BUILDING. City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL 2:00 pm City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW 1. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. The Invocation was delivered by The Reverend Amy Hodge, Pastor, Mt. Zion AME Church. The Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America was led by Mayor Joseph L. Cobb. Welcome ANNOUNCEMENTS: 2. PRESENTATIONS AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: Mayor Cobb advised that, going forward, the 2:00 pm meeting would begin with the Council Members providing "shout-outs" or announcing community events recently attended. The Council Members made the following announcements: Council Member Powers “shouted out” the ribbon cuttings for Urban Commercial Cleaning, LLC, and Spice Titan and expressed excitement about the new businesses in the City of Roanoke. Council Member Volosin “shouted out” the watch party to preview the Renovation Alliance "Buzz4good" episode at the Grandin Theatre, which is the 90th episode that aired on Wednesday, October 28, at 7:00 pm on Blue Ridge PBS. Council Member Nash "shouted-out" his wife as a newly married person and all spouses of City Council members. Vice-Mayor McGuire congratulated Hoot and Holler on their ten-year anniversary; the city's public safety staff for safe city-wide Halloween events; and poll workers for the 45 days of working early voting and announced that Election Day was Tuesday, November 3. Council Member Sanchez-Jones "shouted out" Sheriff Hash on the wellattended Trunk or Treat event held at the Berlgund Center; and the Latinas Network on their Dias de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) event held at the Taubman Museum of Art on November 1, 2026. Council Member Hagen "shouted-out" the Trunk or Treat event held at the newly renovated Eureka Park Recreation Center and advised that 200 children were expected and over 600 hundred were in attendance. Mayor Cobb “shouted out” Angelia Vernon, Assistant to the City Manager, and Adrian Tasco, Human Resources Learning Specialist, for a successful Mayor's Summit held on Thursday, October 29, at Virginia Western Community College. He also acknowledged the City Manager's beautiful remarks delivered at the home going service of Jeffery White, a City employee who passed away on October 18. Presentation by Elevate 11. Withdrawn. Presentation by the Hope and Home Taskforce. Mayor Cobb, Jennifer Huffman, Lee Clark, Cynthia Morrow and Valerie Brown presented the recommendations from the Hope and Home Taskforce. 3. HEARING OF CITIZENS UPON PUBLIC MATTERS: The City Council sets this time as a priority for citizens to be heard. All matters will be referred to the City Manager for response, recommendation or report to the Council, as she may deem appropriate. Citizens spoke prior to Section 2, Presentations and Acknowledgments. Ben Byrd appeared before the Council and spoke with regard to the city government not listening to its people and expressed that a Google or a data center representative had not engaged with the residents prior to negotiations which were completed in secret. Todd Reighley appeared before the Council and spoke with regard to a recent presentation on collective bargaining. He thanked the City Council and City Manager for the presentation and explained that employees want to be heard and share ideas. 4. CONSENT AGENDA: (APPROVED 6-0, Council Member Sanchez-Jones was not present when the vote was recorded.) C-1. Minutes of the regular meetings of City Council held on Monday, September 21, 2026, and on Monday, October 5, 2026. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Dispensed with the reading of the minutes and approved as recorded. C-2. Request to schedule and advertise a public hearing to be held on Monday, November 16, 2026, at 7:00 pm, or as soon thereafter as the matter may be heard, to consider a tax exemption on real property owned by Roanoke Area Ministries. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-3. Request to schedule and advertise a public hearing to be held on Monday, November 16, 2026, at 7:00 pm or as soon as thereafter as the matter may be heard, to consider a request from Roanoke Gas Company for a utility easement along city-owned property located at 304 Reserve Avenue, SW, bearing Tax Map Number 1040202. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-4. Community Meeting announcement to seek public review and comment on the proposed draft update of City Code Chapter 11.8 Erosion and Stormwater Management to be held on Thursday, November 19, 2026, from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. at the City of Roanoke Main Library, 706 S. Jefferson Street, Roanoke, VA 24016. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Received and filed. C-5. Report of qualifications of the following individuals: Anita Price as a member of the Youth Services Citizen Board for a two-year term of office commencing July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2028; Kristin Leary as a member of the Gun Violence Prevention Commission for a term of office ending March 31, 2029; Jonathan Pait as a member of the Youth Services Citizen Board for a one-year term of office commencing July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2027; Karen Pillis as a member of the Youth Services Citizen Board for a three-year term of office commencing July 1, 2026 and ending June 30, 2029; Dawn Erdman as a member of the Board of Zoning Appeals for a three-year term of office, commencing January 1, 2027, and ending December 31, 2029; and Shamaill Ross as a member of the Roanoke Civic Center Commission for a three-year term of office, commencing October 1, 2026, and ending September 30, 2029. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Received and filed. REGULAR AGENDA: 5. PUBLIC HEARINGS: None. 6. PETITIONS AND COMMUNICATIONS: None. 7. REPORTS OF CITY OFFICERS AND THE CITY MANAGER: 1. City Manager: BRIEFINGS: September Monthly Budget Report - 15 minutes. External Agency Update - 15 minutes. Planning, Building and Development Briefing - 15 minutes. Parking Fee Compendium & Ordinance Changes—Parking Study - 15 minutes. ITEMS RECOMMENDED FOR ACTION: a. Acceptance and Appropriation of the Hazardous Materials Team Grant. Adopted Ordinance No. 43489-110226. (7-0) b. Acceptance and Appropriation of the Swift Water Rescue Team Grant. Adopted Ordinance No. 43490-110226. (7-0) c. Acceptance and Appropriation of the Technical Rescue Team Grant. Adopted Ordinance No. 43491-110226. (7-0) d. Acceptance and Appropriation of the Virginia Department of Fire Programs Training Facilities Grant. Adopted Ordinance No. 43492-110226. (7-0) e. Execution of a Performance Agreement between the City of Roanoke, Economic Development Authority of the City of Roanoke and Shadwell Properties, LLC, for costs associated with securing the parking structure located at 33 Salem Avenue SW, Roanoke, VA 24011. Adopted Ordinance No. 43493-110226. (7-0) COMMENTS OF THE CITY MANAGER. The City Manager shared the following comments: I’d like to recognize our Parks and Recreation Department, which recently received three awards at the Virginia Recreation and Park Society’s annual conference in Richmond. The department was recognized for Washington Park Pool as Best New Facility, the Goat Grazing Initiative for Best New Environmental Sustainability, and its creative “Do You Gnome Your Park and Rec Professionals?” campaign for Most Creative Marketing Strategy. Congratulations to everyone involved on this well-deserved recognition. I’d also like to recognize the City employees who participated in our annual Snowfighter training on October 23. Staff from several departments took part in classroom instruction and hands-on exercises to prepare for winter weather, including practicing snow removal techniques and operating large equipment. This training helps ensure our crews are ready to respond safely and efficiently to snow and ice, keeping our roads clear and helping residents get where they need to go throughout the winter season. I would like to take a moment to remind all City employees that Benefits Open Enrollment for the 2027 health plan year is currently underway and will close on Tuesday, November 10th. All benefit-eligible employees must complete their enrollment, even if they plan to keep their current benefits or waive coverage. If you do not make your elections by the deadline, your current benefits will end on December 31, 2026. I’d also like to take a moment to remember Jeff White, our Code Enforcement Officer, who passed away on October 18. Jeff was a valued member of our organization and a respected leader who made a meaningful contribution to our team and the community. He will be greatly missed by his colleagues and all who had the opportunity to work with him. Our thoughts and condolences are with his family, friends, and coworkers during this difficult time. 8. 2. CITY ATTORNEY: None. 3. DIRECTOR OF REAL ESTATE VALUATION: None. REPORTS OF COMMITTEES: 1. Comments on certain Authorities, Boards, Committees and Commissions in which City Council serve as liaisons or appointees. None. 9. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: None. 10. INTRODUCTION AND CONSIDERATION OF ORDINANCES AND RESOLUTIONS: None. 11. MOTIONS AND MISCELLANEOUS BUSINESS: 1. Inquiries and/or comments by the Mayor and Members of City Council. None. 12. RECESSED FOR CONTINUATION OF CLOSED MEETING - 4:18 p.m. 13. RECONVENED - 5:37 p.m. Certification of Closed Meeting. Appointed Mickhal Clary to the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board to replace Mark Jamison for a term of office ending March 31, 2028. Appointed Stephanie Brown-Mead to the Roanoke Neighborhood Advocates for a three-year term of office commencing October 1, 2026, and ending September 30, 2029. Waived the residency requirement for Kiana Bell who was appointed to the Gun Violence Prevention Commission. Waived the residency requirement for Christopher Carver who was appointed to the Roanoke Civic Center Commission. ADJOURNED - 5:39 p.m.

The final vote on the approval of the minutes was for approval 5-0 with Commissioners Donahue and Reid abstaining. REQUEST TO SET PUBLIC HEARINGS N/A PUBLIC HEARINGS REZ 26-01 – JOHNSTON, 2013 CARTERSVILLE ROAD (R-3 TO R-2) Staff presented a rezoning application from Dover Johnston and spouse involving approximately 9.6 acres at 2013 Cartersville Road. The initial request was to rezone the property from R-3 Residential to A-2 Agricultural to permit a two-acre family subdivision for a grandchild. Staff explained that R-3 requires a five-acre minimum lot size and recommended R-2 Residential as a more suitable classification, consistent with existing residential lot patterns. The applicant agreed to the change. Staff discussed the 2023 Comprehensive Plan, proximity to the Cartersville Village Center, separate road frontage for the proposed parcel, and R-2 limitations on agricultural animals. Notices were published October 6 and 13 and mailed to adjoining property owners October 6; staff reported no comments. The Chairman opened the public hearing. No speakers had signed up, and the hearing was closed. MOTION: Commissioner Donahue moved to recommend that the Board of Supervisors approve REZ 26-01, rezoning the property from R-3 Residential to R-2 Residential. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Seal. The motion carried unanimously by a vote of 7–0. 2 PC Minutes 20261019 Page 2 of 6 REZ 26-02 – LAYMAN, CUMBERLAND ROAD (B-2/A-2 TO A-2) Staff presented Mr. Daniel Layman’s request concerning Tax Map Parcels 104-A-13 (approximately 4.97 acres) and 104-A-14 (approximately 5 acres) on Cumberland Road. Each parcel was described as having B-2 Business zoning along the road frontage and A-2 Agricultural zoning toward the rear. The owner requested A-2 zoning for both parcels to construct a dwelling and private shop. Staff reviewed the surrounding zoning, the 2023 Comprehensive Plan, the history of the B-2 district dating to 1994, and nearby uses. In response to discussion of septic suitability, the applicant stated that soil testing had been completed and approved. Notices were published October 6 and 13 and mailed October 6; staff reported no comments. The Chairman opened the public hearing. No speakers had signed up, and the hearing was closed. MOTION: Commissioner Allen moved to recommend approval of REZ 26-02 to the Board of Supervisors, rezoning the B-2 portions of the two parcels to A-2 Agricultural. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Flippen. The motion carried unanimously with a vote of 7–0. OLD BUSINESS POTENTIAL CODE AMENDMENTS Staff reported no new developments. SOLAR PROJECT UPDATE Staff continued working with developers of the Boston Hill and Cumberland solar projects on incomplete site plans, decommissioning plans, and related requirements. Two solar facilities along Cumberland Road were nearing completion. Following heavy rain and sediment-control issues, the Department of Environmental Quality had visited the site, and corrective action was underway. Staff advised that required emergency-vehicle pull-off areas must be completed before final approvals and release of associated erosion and sediment control bonds. 3 PC Minutes 20261019 Page 3 of 6 ROUTE 45 SOUTH SPEED STUDY Staff anticipated receiving information from the Virginia Department of Transportation following the assistant resident engineer’s return from a temporary assignment and planned to provide a later update. REZ 26-03 – DOLLAR GENERAL. Staff reported the applicant withdrew the rezoning request for the Pine Grove Road/Route 60 site and was pursuing a location in Powhatan County. No Commission action was taken. CUP 26-04 – ZYGMUNT CAMPGROUND. Staff reported that the proposed tiny homes on wheels would be treated as recreational vehicles rather than a short-term rental complex. An amended application for an RV campground had been submitted; conditions remained under development. MOTION: Commissioner Allen moved to postpone setting a public hearing for CUP 26-04 until all required documentation was received by the Planning and Zoning Administrator. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Meadows and approved unanimously by a vote of 7–0 BUILDING OPPORTUNITIES ON MAIN STREET (BOOMS) STUDY Staff reviewed preliminary findings from the September 10, 2026 Courthouse-Village walking assessment, attended by approximately 23 participants. Suggested reuse opportunities for the former jail and commercial buildings included museum and visitor functions, professional offices, retail, a pharmacy, food service, residential units, and community amenities. Participants identified needs for sidewalks, crosswalks, health services, public gathering areas, stronger wayfinding to Bear Creek Lake State Park, and possible mixed-use development. The full consultant report is expected later. Commissioners discussed the relationship among investment, housing, population, and economic development. No action was taken. NEW BUSINESS 4 PC Minutes 20261019 Page 4 of 6 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS UPDATE No update was provided in the absence of the Board representative. PLANNING DEPARTMENT REPORT SEPTEMBER 206 • Subdivisions: 10 approved; 48 pending. • Surveys: 20 approved; 31 pending. • Zoning permits: 19 issued. • Residential erosion and sediment control permits: 9 issued. BUILDING INSPECTIONS REPORT – SEPTEMBER 2026 • Permits: 5 new homes, 1 commercial, and 59 other permits. • Certificates of Occupancy: 8 issued. • Fees collected: $8,225.73. • Estimated value of construction: $1,665,271.76. COURTHOUSE VILLAGE SMALL AREA PLAN Staff reported that the Board of Supervisors approved a contract with the Berkeley Group to begin preparation of the Courthouse Village Small Area Plan. Staff discussed potential future ordinance work regarding mixed-use development and village-center planning. SHRINK SWELL SOIL INFORMATION Staff reviewed the County’s approach to expansive soils that may affect foundations and footings. Staff described a 1998 Board policy, the use of GIS mapping to identify potentially affected parcels, early notification during zoning-permit review, and the potential need for sitespecific soil evaluations and engineered foundations. The Commission received a handout that included application materials, consultant information, the adopted policy, and practices in surrounding localities. This item was informational; no action was requested. GENERAL CITIZEN COMMENTS No general citizen comments were offered. 5 PC Minutes 20261019 Page 5 of 6 COMMISSIONER COMMENTS Commissioner Donahue expressed appreciation for staff’s work to bring Planning Commission minutes current and explained his abstention on minutes for meetings he could not recall sufficiently to affirm. He also shared an informal online estimate of Cumberland County home prices in response to an earlier question; the figures were not presented as a verified County statistic. Mr. Reed requested correction of his earlier approval-of-minutes vote to an abstention. No other Commission action is reflected. ADJOURNMENT MOTION: A motion was made by Commissioner Allen to adjourn until the next regular Planning Commission meeting on November 16, 2026, at 6:30 p.m., or as soon thereafter as may be necessary. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Meadows and approved unanimously with a vote of 7-0. The meeting was adjourned at 7:41 p.m. Attested: ___ ___ Planning Commission Chairman Date ___ ___ Planning Director Date 6 PC Minutes 20261019 Page 6 of 6 MINUTES OF THE CUMBERLAND COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING Cumberland County Circuit Courtroom Monday, September 21, 2026 6:30 p.m. PRESENT: Steve Rosen, District 1, Chairman Hubert Allen, District 4, Vice-Chairman Stephen Donahue, District 2 Matthew Seal, District 3 Kevin Meadows, District 5 William Flippen, At-Large Michael Reid, At-Large (arrived at 6:31 p.m.) ALSO PRESENT: Stephany S. Johnson, Planning Director, Zoning Administrator Paul Stimpson, Board of Supervisors Liaison to the Commission ABSENT: None CALL TO ORDER AND ROLL CALL The Chairman called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. Roll call was conducted and a quorum was established. APPROVAL OF AGENDA MOTION: A motion was made by Commissioner Allen and seconded by Commissioner Donahue to approve the agenda. The motion passed 7-0. APPROVAL OF MINUTES The Commission reviewed several months of prior meeting minutes. 7 PC Minutes 20260921 Page 1 of 6 MOTION: Commissioner Allen moved to approve the minutes as presented. Commissioner Flippen seconded. Corrections were identified concerning roll-call language in minutes where a member had been absent and a correction was made to Commissioner Steve Donahue's district designation from District 1 to District 2. Staff stated that the roll-call language would be reviewed and clarified where necessary. MOTION: Commissioner Allen made a substitute motion, seconded by Commissioner Donahue, to approve the minutes as presented with the corrections discussed. The minutes approved were for the Commission meetings from January 8, 2026, January 12, 2026, February 23, 2026, April 20, 2026, May 18, 2026, June 15, 2026, July 20, 2026, July 29, 2026, July 31, 2026, August 10, 2026, August 24, 2026, August 26, 2026, and August 31, 2026. The motion passed 6-0 with Commissioner Reid abstaining. REQUEST TO SET PUBLIC HEARINGS CUP 26-04 - ZIGMUND TINY HOME CAMPGROUND Staff presented a request to set a public hearing for CUP 26-04 concerning a proposed tiny home campground. The applicant proposed using approximately 6.5 acres of a 27-acre tract for three camping areas containing tiny homes on wheels to be rented for short-term stays. Staff explained that the County ordinance defines a short-term rental complex as a camping and overnight area used for temporary habitation and operated as a business or for a fee. The proposed units would remain on wheels and would be connected to electrical service, water, and septic facilities. Health Department approvals would be required for water and wastewater facilities, and electrical permits would be required for service to the sites. Commissioners discussed whether the proposed units should be regulated as a short-term rental complex, campground, or recreational vehicle park. Discussion included whether the units would be subject to building or manufactured-housing standards, licensing and inspection requirements, 8 PC Minutes 20260921 Page 2 of 6 limits on continuous occupancy, and the standards under which the units would be manufactured and transported. Staff offered to obtain additional information from the applicant concerning the construction standards, manufacture, transportation, and regulatory classification of the proposed tiny homes. The applicant would also be asked to attend the next meeting to answer questions. MOTION: A motion was made and seconded to postpone the request to set a public hearing until the next meeting so that additional information could be obtained. The motion passed 6-1, with Commissioner William Flippen voting against. REZONING 26-01 - JOHNSTON Staff presented a request to set a public hearing for Rezoning 26-01. The applicant owns just under 10 acres at the intersection of Ampthill Road and Cartersville Road and requested rezoning from R-3 to A-2. Staff explained that the applicant wished to convey approximately two acres to a grandchild as a family subdivision, which could not be accomplished under the R-3 five-acre minimum lot size. MOTION: Commissioner Allen moved to set Rezoning 26-01 for public hearing on October 19, 2026. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Flippen, and passed unanimously with a vote of 7-0. REZONING 26-02 - LAYMAN Staff presented a request to set a public hearing for Rezoning 26-02. The applicant recently purchased two vacant tracts on Route 45 South, Cumberland Road, believing the property was zoned agricultural. Staff later advised that the parcels were zoned B-2. The applicant requested rezoning from B-2 to A-2 in order to construct a residence and potentially a residential shop. Commissioners discussed the location of the parcels, the history of the B-2 zoning in the area, nearby development, sewer availability, and the potential for residential use. 9 PC Minutes 20260921 Page 3 of 6 MOTION: Commissioner Allen moved to set Rezoning 26-02 for public hearing on October 19, 2026. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Meadows and passed unanimously with a vote of 7-0. PUBLIC HEARINGS None OLD BUSINESS ROUTE 45 SOUTH SPEED STUDY Staff reported that there were no significant updates on old business items. The Route 45 South speed study was expected to be presented to the Board of Supervisors within the next month or two. Staff stated that the information would be shared with the Commission when available. NEW BUSINESS PLANNING DEPARTMENT REPORT Staff presented the Planning Department monthly report. Activity included: • 5 subdivisions approved. • 8 surveys approved. • 28 zoning permits approved. • 9 residential erosion and sediment control permits approved. • No development permits, conditional use permits, or rezoning’s approved during the reporting period. Staff noted that a number of applications remained pending and that older files were being reviewed to determine whether applicants intended to proceed or withdraw their applications. BUILDING INSPECTIONS REPORT The Building Inspections Department reported: 10 PC Minutes 20260921 Page 4 of 6 • 16 new home permits. • 7 commercial permits. • 94 other permits, including electrical, plumbing, mechanical, sheds, carports, and similar permits. • 6 certificates of occupancy. • $19,976.34 in total fees collected. • $4,163,353.33 in total estimated construction value. Staff also reported that Rex and Companies had withdrawn its rezoning application associated with a proposed Dollar General. The application would therefore not come before the Planning Commission. GENERAL CITIZEN COMMENTS None COMMISSIONER COMMENTS Chairman Rosen welcomed Commissioner Michael Reed to the Planning Commission and thanked him for volunteering to serve. Commissioner Flippen commented on the procedure used during the previous public hearing. He recommended that after a main motion is made and seconded, the Chairman expressly call for discussion and provide each Commissioner an opportunity to comment before proceeding to a roll-call vote. Chairman Rosen agreed that the approach would be appropriate. Commissioner Seal noted that larger public meetings also present time-management concerns, particularly when lengthy proceedings result in members of the public leaving before Commissioner comments. Commissioners discussed the importance of providing each member an opportunity to speak while managing larger meetings efficiently. ADJOURNMENT MOTION: A motion was made by Commissioner Allen to adjourn until the next regular Planning Commission meeting on October 19, 2026, at 6:30 p.m., or as soon thereafter as may be 11 PC Minutes 20260921 Page 5 of 6 necessary. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Donahue and approved unanimously with a vote of 7-0. Avoid during public meetings and during the performance of public duties the-use of abusive, threatening or intimidating language or gestures directed at colleagues, citizens, or personnel. 2. Pay all taxes due to the County, state, or national government. 3. Avoid a private lifestyle that casts public doubt upon the integrity and competence of the County government. 4. Make a conscientious effort to be well prepared for each meeting . 5. Recognizing the dignity of each individual, the Board shall attempt to avoid offering public criticism of colleagues or County employees . 6. Work to create a positive environment in public meeting where citizens will feel comfortable in their roles as observers or participants. 7. Maintain an attitude of courtesy and consideration toward all colleagues and staff during all discussions and deliberations. 8. Be tolerant. Allow citizens, employees, or colleagues sufficient opportunity to present their views. 9. Be respectful and attentive. Avoid comments, body language or distracting activity that conveys a message of disrespect for the presentations from citizens, personnel, or colleagues . Be concise. 10. Avoid the practice of taking more time to address an issue before the body than is necessary and essential for an adequate consideration of those matters being discussed. Board members should always remember, "There is no right way to do the wrong thing." HALIFAX COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS CONDUCT OF THE PUBLIC The efficient and dignified conduct of public business is an ultimate concern of the Board. Accordingly, it is the policy of the Board that its meetings be conducted with the highest degree of order and decorum. The Board's integrity and dignity will be established and maintained at all times during the conduct of public business, and the Board will permit no behavior which is not in keeping with this policy. Prohibited conduct at meetings shall include: 1. 2. 3. Campaigning for public office, soliciting of funds, or promoting private business ventures. Using profanity, vulgar language or gestures. Language or actions which insult or demean any person or group of persons or which, when directed at a public official or employee is not related to his official duties. 4. Disruptive behavior. 5. Making non-germane or frivolous statements. 6. Discussions of a sectarian or partisan nature. 7. Smoking or eating in the Board Room . 8. Addressing question or statements to anyone other than the Chairman (Questions shall be presented to the Chairman, who will, at their discretion, solicit a response from the appropriate board or staff member.) 9. Standing in the back or side isles of the Board Room as long as there are sufficient seats available (except for law enforcement personnel). 10. Persons in attendance at the meeting addressing the Board while members of the Board are considering any motion, resolution or ordinance preliminary to a vote on the same, except at the discretion of the Chairman. 11. Any persons addressing comments or questions to someone other than the Chairman . 12. Wearing hats, caps or other types of headgear. 13. Applause is permitted only during presentations, awards, proclamations and special recognition periods. The Board of Supervisors welcomes and encourages citizen participation in its meetings. To insure fair and timely participation, the following procedures are observed by the Board: 1. 2. All presenters are asked to state their name Each speaker on a general matter, whether an individual or a representative for an organization, is limited to three (3) minutes. 3. Speaker's comments are limited to a presentation on his or her point of view only - questions of clarification may be entertained only by the board members; 4. All comments are to be directed to the board; 5. Debate between a recognized speaker and audience members or between board members and the speaker is not permitted; 6. Courtesy between the speaker and audience is expected at all times; 7. Speakers are requested to leave any written statement and/ or comments with the clerk to the board; 8. Individuals speaking on behalf of an organized group are required to file with the clerk written authorization from the group allowing the individual to represent that group; 9. By applying to speak as a representative for an organization, the individual confirms they are recognized as an official representative of that organization; and 10. Presentation to the board by groups should: a. Obtain prior approval from the chairman of the board; b. Submit all written materials and data no later than ten days prior to the meeting in time to be included in the board's agenda packet distributed a week before each regular monthly meeting; c. Limit presentations to fifteen minutes; and d. File with the clerk written authorization from the group allowing the individual to represent that group. 11 . A digital , color-coded timer will be displayed in full view of the Board, the speaker, and individuals seated in the gallery. When two minutes have expired, the timer display will turn yellow indicating the speaker has one minute to conclude his/her comments . At the end of that one-minute period (completion of the full three-minute period), the timer will display 0:00 in red, indicating the speaker must relinquish the podium to the next speaker. Staff will notify the Chairman that the speaker's time has expired. Speakers continuing after the time allotted shall be ruled out of order by the Chairman. The Chairman shall preserve order and decorum at all meetings. The Chairman may order the expulsion of any person for violation of these rules, disruptive behavior, or any words or action which incite violence or disorder, subject to appeal to the Board. Any person so expelled shall not be readmitted for the remainder of the meeting from which he was expelled. Any person who has been so expelled and who at a later meeting again engages in words or actions justifying expulsion may be barred from attendance at future meetings of the Board for a specified and reasonable period of time not to exceed six months or upon a still subsequent expulsion , a period not to exceed one year either by the Chairman , subject to appeal to the Board, or by motion passed by the Board . BUSINESS ITEMS PS - HALIF OUNTY AGENDA BRIEFING Staff Members: Meeting Date: November 17, 2026 Detrick Easley Item# D-1 Ordinance# Department: Subject: Planning & Zoning Legal status of plan § 15. 2-2232 review Wolftrap Solar, Parcel;13797 4.9MWac Facility Background: Virginia Code § 15.2-2232 requires the local Planning Commission and governing body to determine whether the general location, character, and extent of a proposed public utility facility or other covered public facility are substantially in accordance with the County's adopted Comprehensive Plan. RC DEVCO, LLC, on behalf of Wolftrap Solar/Agrisolar, has submitted an application for a Conditional Use Permit to construct and operate a 4.9 MWac solar energy facility (the "Project") on one parcel located in Board of Supervisors District 5. The subject property is identified as Halifax County Parcel Identification Number 13 797, contains approximately 42.88 acres, and is owned by Ronnie and Joyce Green. Existing Land Use The subject parcel currently consists of managed timberland, agricultural hay production areas, and open fields. The Applicant proposes to maintain agricultural viability through site restoration requirements and agrivoltaic practices, including sheep grazing within the solar facility. P6 Future Land Use The Halifax County 2017-2037 Comprehensive Plan identifies the subject property for continued agricultural use. Comprehensive Plan and Surrounding Land Use The Halifax County Comprehensive Plan recognizes and encourages the development of renewable energy resources when appropriately located and designed to minimize impacts on surrounding properties and the County's rural character. The Comprehensive Plan includes policies that: • • • • Promote appropriately located renewable energy facilities, including solar and wind energy generation and battery storage, in a manner consistent with the Commonwealth Energy Policy and the other provisions of the Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. Encourage appropriately sited electric generation and transmission facilities, as well as pipeline infrastructure. Promote the protection of rural scenic roads and byways through appropriate land development practices. Encourage the preservation of existing vegetation and natural screening to minimize visibility from roadways, residences, lakes, streams, and rivers. The surrounding properties are zoned R-1 Residential. Accordingly, appropriate setbacks, vegetative screening, and other site-specific conditions should be considered to minimize potential impacts on adjacent residential properties. P7 Staff Considerations The proposed Wolftrap Solar facility represents a renewable energy development within an area designated for agricultural use by the Comprehensive Plan. The Applicant's proposed agrivoltaic practices, including sheep grazing, are intended to maintain an agricultural component of the property while allowing for renewable energy production. The Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors must consider the general location, character, and extent of the proposed facility in determining whether the Project is substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232. Recommended Motions First Motion - I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A), that the Halifax County Planning Commission find that the general location, character, and extent of the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility, located on Parcel Identification Number 13797 in Board of Supervisors District 5, are substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. Second Motion - Communication of Finding I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(B), that the Planning Commission direct the Zoning Administrator to communicate its findings regarding the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility to the Halifax County Board of Supervisors for consideration. Motion to Deny - Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A) I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A), that the Halifax County Planning Commission find that the general location, character, and extent of the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility, located on Parcel Identification Number 13797 in District 5, are not substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. This recommendation is based on concerns regarding the compatibility of the proposed solar facility with the surrounding land uses and the residential character of the area. The subject property is surrounded by properties zoned R-1 Residential. The proposed development may create land-use compatibility concerns and potential impacts on neighboring residential properties. The Planning Commission finds that the proposed location does not adequately demonstrate compatibility with the surrounding residential development and the Comprehensive Plan's goals of protecting rural character and promoting appropriately located development. PS Second Motion - Communication of Finding I move, pursuant to Virginia Code§ 15.2-2232(B), that the Zoning Administrator be directed to communicate the Planning Commission's finding of noncompliance with the Halifax County Board of Supervisors. P9 - PUBLIC HEARINGS HALI OUNTY Staff Report Staff Members: Meeting Date: November 17, 2026 Detrick Easley Item# E-1 Ordinance# Article VII Department: Planning & Zoning Subject: Conditional Use Permit (CUP) Review: Wolftrap Solar, 4.9MWac Facility BACKGROUND RC DEVCO, LLC, on behalf ofWolftrap Solar/Agrisolar, has submitted an application for a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) to construct and operate a solar energy facility (the "Project") on one parcel located in Board of Supervisors District 5. The subject property is identified as Parcel Record Number 13797 and contains approximately 42.88 acres. The proposed facility will have a generating capacity ofup to 4.9 megawatts alternating current (MWac) and will connect to an existing 34.5-kilovolt distribution circuit located within the Project area. No battery energy storage system (BESS) is currently proposed as part of this Project. STAFF COMMENTS AND ANALYSIS Staff and the Berkley Group have reviewed and evaluated the application against the applicable review criteria and additional considerations established by the County's Solar Facilities Ordinance. The review considers whether the proposed Project adequately protects County view sheds and natural resources, safeguards the health, safety, and welfare of the community, and otherwise advances the purpose and intent of the Solar Facilities Article. Pll The following summarizes the findings and considerations associated with the proposed development: 1. The proposed location is outside identified industrial growth corridors. However, the Comprehensive Plan amendment addressing renewable energy recognizes rural areas with available transmission infrastructure as potential locations for appropriately sited solar facilities. Within the half-mile review area, no known architectural resources were identified. No resources within the review area are considered eligible or potentially eligible for listing on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) or the Virginia Landmarks Register (VLR). Any additional coordination or review required by the Virginia Department of Historic Resources shall be completed prior to construction. P12 4. Proximity to Other Energy Facilities and Utility Infrastructure Staff/Berkley Group finds that the proposed solar facility would support the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan by expanding the County's renewable energy infrastructure. The Project would contribute to the County's utility network and provide an additional source of energy generation. Potential impacts to the natural environment are expected to be evaluated and addressed through applicable permit requirements and project conditions. 5. Scenic Resources, Waterways, and Natural Resources With respect to proximity to, visibility from, and potential impacts on areas of scenic significance, including scenic byways, vistas, and blue ways, a review of the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation's (DCR) Natural Heritage Data Explorer identified waterways within the Project site or within two miles of the property. These ratings indicate that land-disturbance activities within the Project area have an elevated potential to affect downstream aquatic resources. The Applicant proposes to minimize impacts to wetlands and surface waters and comply with applicable setbacks from water resources. The Applicant has also indicated that storm water management and water-quality compliance will be addressed through coordination with the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ). Upon decommissioning, the Applicant will be required to restore the soil and vegetation to conditions that are equal to or better than the existing conditions, consistent with … to have plantings for screening to minimize visual impacts on neighboring properties. A telecommunications tower and its associated facilities are located on the site and will remain operational throughout the life of the solar project. … During construction, access to the site will be via the maintenance road to the existing telecommunications tower on the site off Bellevue Road, State Route 729. After commissioning, access to the project will be provided via a proposed … governing the siting and development of solar energy facilities . Avoid during public meetings and during the performance of public duties the-use of abusive, threatening or intimidating language or gestures directed at colleagues, citizens, or personnel. 2. Pay all taxes due to the County, state, or national government. 3. Avoid a private lifestyle that casts public doubt upon the integrity and competence of the County government. 4. Make a conscientious effort to be well prepared for each meeting . 5. Recognizing the dignity of each individual, the Board shall attempt to avoid offering public criticism of colleagues or County employees . 6. Work to create a positive environment in public meeting where citizens will feel comfortable in their roles as observers or participants. 7. Maintain an attitude of courtesy and consideration toward all colleagues and staff during all discussions and deliberations. 8. Be tolerant. Allow citizens, employees, or colleagues sufficient opportunity to present their views. 9. Be respectful and attentive. Avoid comments, body language or distracting activity that conveys a message of disrespect for the presentations from citizens, personnel, or colleagues . Be concise. 10. Avoid the practice of taking more time to address an issue before the body than is necessary and essential for an adequate consideration of those matters being discussed. Board members should always remember, "There is no right way to do the wrong thing." HALIFAX COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS CONDUCT OF THE PUBLIC The efficient and dignified conduct of public business is an ultimate concern of the Board. Accordingly, it is the policy of the Board that its meetings be conducted with the highest degree of order and decorum. The Board's integrity and dignity will be established and maintained at all times during the conduct of public business, and the Board will permit no behavior which is not in keeping with this policy. Prohibited conduct at meetings shall include: 1. 2. 3. Campaigning for public office, soliciting of funds, or promoting private business ventures. Using profanity, vulgar language or gestures. Language or actions which insult or demean any person or group of persons or which, when directed at a public official or employee is not related to his official duties. 4. Disruptive behavior. 5. Making non-germane or frivolous statements. 6. Discussions of a sectarian or partisan nature. 7. Smoking or eating in the Board Room . 8. Addressing question or statements to anyone other than the Chairman (Questions shall be presented to the Chairman, who will, at their discretion, solicit a response from the appropriate board or staff member.) 9. Standing in the back or side isles of the Board Room as long as there are sufficient seats available (except for law enforcement personnel). 10. Persons in attendance at the meeting addressing the Board while members of the Board are considering any motion, resolution or ordinance preliminary to a vote on the same, except at the discretion of the Chairman. 11. Any persons addressing comments or questions to someone other than the Chairman . 12. Wearing hats, caps or other types of headgear. 13. Applause is permitted only during presentations, awards, proclamations and special recognition periods. The Board of Supervisors welcomes and encourages citizen participation in its meetings. To insure fair and timely participation, the following procedures are observed by the Board: 1. 2. All presenters are asked to state their name Each speaker on a general matter, whether an individual or a representative for an organization, is limited to three (3) minutes. 3. Speaker's comments are limited to a presentation on his or her point of view only - questions of clarification may be entertained only by the board members; 4. All comments are to be directed to the board; 5. Debate between a recognized speaker and audience members or between board members and the speaker is not permitted; 6. Courtesy between the speaker and audience is expected at all times; 7. Speakers are requested to leave any written statement and/ or comments with the clerk to the board; 8. Individuals speaking on behalf of an organized group are required to file with the clerk written authorization from the group allowing the individual to represent that group; 9. By applying to speak as a representative for an organization, the individual confirms they are recognized as an official representative of that organization; and 10. Presentation to the board by groups should: a. Obtain prior approval from the chairman of the board; b. Submit all written materials and data no later than ten days prior to the meeting in time to be included in the board's agenda packet distributed a week before each regular monthly meeting; c. Limit presentations to fifteen minutes; and d. File with the clerk written authorization from the group allowing the individual to represent that group. 11 . A digital , color-coded timer will be displayed in full view of the Board, the speaker, and individuals seated in the gallery. When two minutes have expired, the timer display will turn yellow indicating the speaker has one minute to conclude his/her comments . At the end of that one-minute period (completion of the full three-minute period), the timer will display 0:00 in red, indicating the speaker must relinquish the podium to the next speaker. Staff will notify the Chairman that the speaker's time has expired. Speakers continuing after the time allotted shall be ruled out of order by the Chairman. The Chairman shall preserve order and decorum at all meetings. The Chairman may order the expulsion of any person for violation of these rules, disruptive behavior, or any words or action which incite violence or disorder, subject to appeal to the Board. Any person so expelled shall not be readmitted for the remainder of the meeting from which he was expelled. Any person who has been so expelled and who at a later meeting again engages in words or actions justifying expulsion may be barred from attendance at future meetings of the Board for a specified and reasonable period of time not to exceed six months or upon a still subsequent expulsion , a period not to exceed one year either by the Chairman , subject to appeal to the Board, or by motion passed by the Board . Existing Land Use The subject parcel currently consists of managed timberland, agricultural hay production areas, and open fields. The Applicant proposes to maintain agricultural viability through site restoration requirements and agrivoltaic practices, including sheep grazing within the solar facility. P6 Future Land Use The Halifax County 2017-2037 Comprehensive Plan identifies the subject property for continued agricultural use. Comprehensive Plan and Surrounding Land Use The Halifax County Comprehensive Plan recognizes and encourages the development of renewable energy resources when appropriately located and designed to minimize impacts on surrounding properties and the County's rural character. The Comprehensive Plan includes policies that: • • • • Promote appropriately located renewable energy facilities, including solar and wind energy generation and battery storage, in a manner consistent with the Commonwealth Energy Policy and the other provisions of the Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. Encourage appropriately sited electric generation and transmission facilities, as well as pipeline infrastructure. Promote the protection of rural scenic roads and byways through appropriate land development practices. Encourage the preservation of existing vegetation and natural screening to minimize visibility from roadways, residences, lakes, streams, and rivers. The surrounding properties are zoned R-1 Residential. Accordingly, appropriate setbacks, vegetative screening, and other site-specific conditions should be considered to minimize potential impacts on adjacent residential properties. The Applicant's proposed agrivoltaic practices, including sheep grazing, are intended to maintain an agricultural component of the property while allowing for renewable energy production. The Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors must consider the general location, character, and extent of the proposed facility in determining whether the Project is substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232. Recommended Motions First Motion - I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A), that the Halifax County Planning Commission find that the general location, character, and extent of the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility, located on Parcel Identification Number 13797 in Board of Supervisors District 5, are substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. Second Motion - Communication of Finding I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(B), that the Planning Commission direct the Zoning Administrator to communicate its findings regarding the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility to the Halifax County Board of Supervisors for consideration. Motion to Deny - Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A) I move, pursuant to Virginia Code § 15.2-2232(A), that the Halifax County Planning Commission find that the general location, character, and extent of the proposed Wolftrap Solar facility, located on Parcel Identification Number 13797 in District 5, are not substantially in accordance with the adopted Halifax County Comprehensive Plan. This recommendation is based on concerns regarding the compatibility of the proposed solar facility with the surrounding land uses and the residential character of the area. The subject property is surrounded by properties zoned R-1 Residential. The proposed development may create land-use compatibility concerns and potential impacts on neighboring residential properties. The Planning Commission finds that the proposed location does not adequately demonstrate compatibility with the surrounding residential development and the Comprehensive Plan's goals of protecting rural character and promoting appropriately located development. PS Second Motion - Communication of Finding I move, pursuant to Virginia Code§ 15.2-2232(B), that the Zoning Administrator be directed to communicate the Planning Commission's finding of noncompliance with the Halifax County Board of Supervisors. Planning Commission Holiday Dinner - December 10, 2026 Hanover County Planning Commission Public Hearing Rules The purpose of public hearings is to allow the public an opportunity to speak to the Commission on matters within its purview, including rezoning and conditional use permit requests, zoning and subdivision ordinance amendments, and comprehensive plan amendments. Comments made by speakers must relate to the matter being discussed, and all comments must be directed to the Commission. Questions posed by speakers will generally be answered at the end of the hearing by either the Commission or staff. During the public hearing, members of the Commission may ask questions of speakers to clarify comments or obtain other relevant information. The Commission may also ask any speaker questions for clarification after the public hearing has been closed. The procedure for a public hearing is as follows: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. Planning Department staff will give a presentation outlining the request and staff’s recommendations. The applicant and/or his representative will have up to fifteen (15) minutes to make their presentation. The applicant or representative of the applicant may reserve up to five (5) minutes of the time allotted for its presentation for use as rebuttal time. After the applicant’s presentation, other proponents will have up to fifteen (15) minutes to speak, for a maximum of five (5) minutes each. Thereafter, opponents of the application will also have up to fifteen (15) minutes to speak, for a maximum of five (5) minutes each. Time consumed by the Commission asking questions and a speaker’s responses will not count against these limits. Proponents and opponents may not yield their allotted time to other speakers. If the Chairman determines that the issues involved are unusually complex, or that a large number of persons desire to speak, these time limits may be adjusted, provided that the amount of time will be allotted equally to proponents and opponents. After the applicant, proponents, and opponents have spoken, the Chairman will declare the public hearing closed and the Commission will then deliberate and vote on the application. No public hearing may extend beyond two (2) hours unless approved by majority vote of the Commission. All speakers and others in the meeting room must maintain proper decorum and demonstrate civility toward the Commission, staff, applicants, and the public at large. The Chairman shall be responsible for enforcing the rules of the Planning Commission, including those related to decorum and civility. All Planning Commission meetings are streamed live. To access the live stream, visit our website at www.hanovercounty.gov. Hanover: People, Tradition and Spirit
