Roll call was taken with member Sherrin Alsop being absent. PPROVAL OF WARRANTS A motion was made by Mr. Simpkins and seconded by Ms. Norman to approve the August 24, 2026 warrants subject to audit. AYES: J.L. SIMPKINS, M. R. BERRY, M.H. NORMAN, C.R. BILLUPS NAYS: NONE ABSENT: S.C. ALSOP PROCLAMATION – OCTOBER AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH/THRIVE VIRGINIA Representatives from Thrive Virginia provided information on the programs and services offered in King and Queen County and presented information on the promotion of October being designated as Domestic Violence Awareness month. A motion was made by Ms. Norman and seconded by Ms. Billups to adopt the following proclamation: . PROCLAMATI ON 2026 A PROCLAMATION DECLARING OCTOBER AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH 1 WHEREAS, domestic violence is a serious crime that affects people of all races, ages, gender, and income levels; and WHEREAS, Domestic violence is widespread and affects over four million Americans each year; and WHEREAS, one in three Americans have witnessed an incident of domestic violence; and WHEREAS, children that grow up in violent homes are believed to be abused and neglected at a rate higher than the national average; and WHEREAS, domestic violence costs the nation billions of dollars annually in medical expenses, police and court costs, shelters, foster care, sick leave, absenteeism, and non- productivity; and WHEREAS, only a coordinated community effort will put a stop to this heinous crime; and. WHEREAS, Domestic Violence Awareness Month provides an excellent opportunity for citizens to learn more about preventing domestic violence and to show support for the numerous organizations and individuals who provide critical advocacy, services, and assistance to victims. NOW, THEREFORE, IT IS PROCLAIMED by the King and Queen County Board of Supervisors the month of October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month and ask the citizens of King and Queen County to work together to eliminate domestic violence from our community. Mark Berry, Board Chairman AYES: J.L. SIMPKINS, M. R. BERRY, M.H. NORMAN, C.R. BILLUPS NAYS: NONE ABSENT: S.C. ALSOP JOINT DISCUSSION – ELEMENTARY SCHOOL PROJECT Chairman Berry provided the following update from the work group on the elementary school project: • There were five responses to the RFQ for the Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR). • The work group decided to move four of the five forward to the next step in the process. Letters have been sent to the four contractors, and it is expected that the RFP will go out this week. • The amendment to the Grimm + Parker contract is scheduled to occur at the October board meeting. They will continue to work on the project alongside whichever contractor is selected. • It is still anticipated to break ground in the spring of 2027. Ms. Billups added the following comments: • There have been a lot of things going on in the background even though it may 2 • look like the project is not progressing. The have been obstacles to overcome and the board wants to make sure that it is done correctly. Once the project actually gets to the construction phase, that will be the easy part. Ms. Norman thanked the work group for all of their work to keep the project moving. Other counties are watching how it progresses. Mr. Simpkins commented that he is glad to see the project moving forward. Although it is taking a long time, it won’t be as long as it has been. The following comments were made by the School Board: Mr. Hill noted that he is glad that something is being done, the children are tired of being in the modulars. Ms. Gaines stated that the children are excited, they are bringing their parents along with the one school idea. Dr. Carter said that she is excited that the children will get this opportunity. JOINT DISCUSSION – PROMOTION OF 1% LOCAL SALES TAX REFERENDUM Chairman Berry advised that the General Assembly approved legislation allowing localities to adopt a 1% local sales tax to be used for school construction. It must be passed by referendum by the citizens of the county. The board has taken the necessary action to have it on the ballot for the November election. He noted that the estimated revenue will be $450,000/year which is approximately .04 on the real estate levy. Both boards agreed to promote the approval of the referendum. It was agreed to keep it simple and focus on the fact that it will help the school division meet their capital needs. JOINT DISCUSSION – SCHOOL BUDGET UPDATE Dr. Carter provided a presentation on the school division’s FY27 budget. The original budget request was for $12,733,381.48 that included $4,656,724.48 in local funds. This was an increase of $289,548.48 in local funds over FY26. Once the state adopted the budget and set the revenue based on the current ADM, the school division has amended their budget to be $12,608,249.48 which still calls for a local increase of $289,548.48. The FY27 budget adopted by the board of supervisors only includes an increase of $50,000 for a total local share of $4,417,176. She noted that the division has already made many cuts such as eliminating positions, combining bus routes and reduced purchase services. She asked that the board fund the remaining $239,549 that was not included in the original budget adopted. After lengthy discussion a motion was made by Mr. Simpkins and seconded by Ms. Norman to approve a budget amendment in the amount of $125,000 in local funds to the school division for a total local share of $4,537,176. AYES: J.L. SIMPKINS, M. R. BERRY, M.H. NORMAN, C.R. BILLUPS NAYS: NONE 3 ABSENT: S.C. ALSOP The School Board adjourned their meeting at this time. DISCUSSION – MONN REGIONAL RADIO SYSTEM It was the consensus of the board to have this discussion placed on the agenda of the October 13th regular board meeting. COUNTY ADMINISTRATOR’S COMMENTS Ms. Seay had no comments. BOARD OF SUPERVISOR’S COMMENTS Mr. Berry thanked everyone for coming. Mr. Simpkins inquired about the Synagro meeting being held at the library tonight. It was noted that Ms. Alsop attended that meeting on behalf of the county, which is why she was not in attendance here. NORMAN NAYS: NONE PUBLIC HEARING – ZA25-01 CHESAPEAKE BAY OVERLAY DISTRICT Chairman Berry asked the Director of Community Development to provide proof of publication and background information. 1 Ms. Sprouse advised that the public hearing was properly advertised in the Tidewater Review and Rappahannock Times. The purpose of the public hearing is to amend Article 12 of the zoning ordinance to include new legislation requirements to address coastal resiliency and adaptation due to sea-level rise and climate change when considering proposed development in the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Area. Chairman Berry opened the public hearing. No comments were received; the public hearing was closed. A motion was made by Ms. Simpkins and seconded by Ms. Norman to accept the recommendation from the Planning Commission and approve the zoning text amendment ZA2501 Article 12, Chesapeake Bay Overlay District. PUBLIC HEARING – CUP26-02 – THE TOWERS, LLC (VERTICAL BRIDGE) & CELLCO PARTNERSHIP (VERIZON WIRELESS) Chairman Berry asked the Director of Community Development to provide proof of publication and background information. Ms. Sprouse advised that the public hearing was properly advertised in the Tidewater Review and the Rappahannock Times. The conditional use permit request is for the installation of a wireless communications tower in the Newtown Magisterial District at the intersection of Minter Lane and Canterbury Road. The proposal was for a self-supporting tower 195’ in height with a 4’ lightning rod for a total height of 199’ with associated equipment located inside a 45’ x 45’ fenced compound. After the Planning Commission public hearing, the applicant has addressed the concerns that were raised by citizens and adjoining landowners. The type of tower has changed from a self-supported lattice style to a self-supported monopole, and the tower will not be marked or lit. The Planning Commission’s recommendation for approval included nine conditions. Chairman Berry opened the public hearing. Lisa Murphy, attorney representing the applicant provided a presentation giving background on the request, the expanded use of wireless technology requiring the addition of more wireless tower sites and a detail of the site and conditions. 2 Peter Cinq-Mars, Buena Vista District – Asked the applicant representative whether there would be generators and batteries on the site. When she responded “yes” he expressed his concern with noise from the generator and the fire risk of batteries being on site. Bette Albert, St. Stephens Church District – She expressed her appreciation to Verizon for working with the citizens on their concerns and requests. She is also glad there will be no lights on the tower. Ann Glubiak, St. Stephens Church District – She noted that she is an adjacent landowner to the project. She also expressed her appreciation to Verizon for working with her on her concerns. She feels that the project preserves rural aesthetics and the changes that were made are meaningful. There being no further comments the public hearing was closed. A motion was made by Mr. Simpkins and seconded by Ms. Alsop to accept the recommendation from the Planning Commission and approve CUP26-02 with the revised nine conditions. AYES: S.C. ALSOP, J.L. SIMPKINS, M.R. BERRY, C.R. BILLUPS, M.H. There is not a concern at this time that this will happen with this application, but this request is to prevent this from being in an issue as the application moves through the process. A motion was made by Ms. Alsop and seconded by Ms. Norman to approve the extension of action by the Planning Commission of CUP26-03. AYES: S.C. ALSOP, J.L. SIMPKINS, M.R. BERRY, C.R. BILLUPS, M.H. The following report summarizes this work and upcoming matters as of November 6, 2026. Notice of Violations (Enforcement) Staff continues to investigate potential zoning violations and work toward voluntary compliance, with referral to the County Attorney when formal enforcement is necessary. Open Notice of Violation Investigations 4 Notice of Violations Awaiting Response/Working Towards Voluntary Compliance 9 Notice of Violations Referred to County Attorney 1 Planning Commission Accessory dwelling units. The Planning Commission continues to review proposed amendments to allow accessory dwelling units in the A-1 and C-1 zoning districts. This work follows adoption of the accessory dwelling unit provisions for the R-1, R-2, and R-3 districts. Sign ordinance. The Planning Commission is developing a proposed repeal and replacement of Article 12, the County’s sign ordinance. Review remains ongoing. Home occupations and rural services. The Planning Commission subcommittee chaired by Anne Gore is developing the proposed ordinance. This initiative remains part of the Commission's ordinance work program. Professional Development. Planning Commission Chair Zachary Whitman, Planning Commission member Anne Gore, and Planning and Zoning Administrator Allen Nicholls completed Virginia Commonwealth University’s Certified Planning Commissioner program and received their CPC designations on October 30, 2026. Active Rezoning Applications 0 Pending Rezoning Applications 0 Ordinance Amendments 3 Pending Special Use Permit Application 0 Administrative Review Page 1 of 3 Return to Agenda Staff continues to review subdivisions and site plans and assist property owners, surveyors, attorneys, appraisers, and real estate professionals with development questions. Recent work has included subdivision potential, entrance and septic requirements, zoning verification, agricultural and event uses, and building setbacks. Subdivision review and development potential. Staff reviewed preliminary subdivision concepts involving public-road frontage, individual entrances, and shared private roads. These reviews consider parcel acreage, division history, zoning limitations, existing access arrangements, and required agency approvals. Staff also addressed family subdivision requirements, including Health Department approval of drainfield and reserve areas for each proposed lot, and coordinated subdivision plat revisions and responses to VDOT and Health Department comments. Zoning verification and property research. Staff researched zoning classifications, rezoning records, proffers, and special use permit history in response to property marketing and appraisal inquiries. Recent assistance included explaining the distinction between zoning and tax assessment classifications, reviewing how existing proffers may affect prospective business uses, and evaluating the zoning status of a longstanding agricultural processing operation. Agricultural, commercial, and event uses. Staff assisted owners and prospective operators with questions about agricultural activities, seasonal events, and potential event venues. Guidance addressed the distinction between limited events permitted by right and operations requiring a special use permit, along with the preliminary development review process. Staff also responded to inquiries about potential adult-use cannabis retail, with further guidance pending clarification of state requirements. Residential development and utilities. Staff evaluated preliminary residential development concepts and explained applicable dwelling classifications, density standards, and public utility requirements. These discussions emphasized that future sewer service cannot be assumed for a prospective acquisition and that development potential remains subject to review of the specific property and proposal. Permit review and setback compliance. Staff reviewed proposed accessory structures and issued written determinations where proposed locations did not meet required front setbacks. Correspondence explained the applicable setback measurements and available procedures for revised siting, variance requests, and appeals. Preliminary Development Review Committee. The November 3 rd meeting was cancelled because there were no applications or cases requiring committee review. Active Subdivision Applications Active Site Plan Applications 7 5 Board of Zoning Appeals The Board of Zoning Appeals currently has no cases scheduled for consideration. The BZA continues to address administrative matters. The Board is close to adopting formal bylaws, as it currently operates without adopted bylaws. Appeal Applications 0 Variance Applications 0 Other Departmental Activities Staff continues to coordinate with the Building Department, County Administration, County Attorney, and reviewing agencies on development proposals and ordinance initiatives. Routine assistance includes interpreting permitted uses, reviewing access and parcel configurations, and explaining application procedures before applicants commit to a project. Comprehensive Plan Subcommittee Report Open Citizen Comment Period Chairman’s Report Clerk’s Report Adjourn Josh Hahn Tracy Clatterbuck Cathy Grech COUNTY OF PAGE 103 South Court Street, Suite F Luray, Virginia 22835 (540) 743-4142 Fax: (540) 743-4533 Board of Supervisors: Clifton ”Bucky” Thomas -Chairman -AtLarge Jeremy Baldwin -District 1 Allen Louderback - District 2 Ryan Cubbage -District 3 Susan Kile -District 4 Jeff Vaughan -District 5 County Administrator: Amity Moler TO: Page County Planning Commission FROM: Tracy Clatterbuck, Zoning Administrator I SUBJECT: Flowerdew Hundred LLC- Special Use Permit Application (Public Hearing) DATE: November 2, 2026 SUMMARY: Special use permit (SUP) to operate a self-storage facility. BACKGROUND: Flowerdew Hundred LLC has filed an application for a special use permit (SUP) to construct a self-storage facility located off US Hwy 340, Stanley, VA, and further identified by tax map number 59-(A)-63F. The parcel of land, currently vacant, is located west of Stanley, approximately 0.8 mile north of US HWY BSN 340 W and just to the north of 2845 US Hwy 340 Stanley. The property contains 9.69 acres and is currently zoned as Agriculture (A-1). The applicant is proposing to construct a self-storage facility for up to 500 self-serve storage units in a mix of the following sizes: 5x5, 5x10, 10x10, 10x15, 10x20, and 10x30. Under Section 125-4 of the Page County Zoning Ordinance, self-storage is defined as follows: SELF STORAGE: A structure or structures containing separate storage spaces of varying sizes leased or rented as individual leases for the purpose of storing personal property and household goods. In the A-1 zoning district, pursuant to Section 125-10.D(19) of the Page County Zoning Ordinance, self-storage units require a SUP. Also, the applicant will be required to comply with the following supplemental code regulations found under Section 125-30.19 (Self-Storage Facilities) of the Page County Zoning Ordinance: A. No commercial activities of any kind shall occur within the facility other than rental of storage units. No repair of vehicles, furniture, or other materials or equipment shall occur within the facility. Signs shall be posted within the facility describing such limitations. B. No storage of hazardous, toxic or explosive materials shall occur in the self-storage facility. Signs shall be posted within the facility describing such limitations. C. The maximum size of any individual storage space or unit in a self-storage facility shall be 500 square feet. D. In the Agriculture Zoning District, fencing, screening, and security may be required for all facilities. Additional conditions may also be required as part of the special use permit review process. E. Self-storage facilities shall not include portable storage containers, shipping containers and/or tractor trailers. The applicant has provided a detailed narrative explaining the proposal along with a concept plan and comp plan references. Draft conditions are included in the packet for review and consideration. As indicated in the supplemental regulations listed above, additional conditions may also be considered relating to fencing, screening, and security. OTHER AGENCY COMMENTS: Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT) – Per Lindsey Burgess with VDOT: 1) The location of the proposed commercial entrance meets VDOT requirements for sight distance. 2) Any access to a state-maintained roadway must be in accordance with Appendix F of the VDOT Road Design Manual. 3) At the site plan phase, VDOT will review and require the design of the new commercial entrance to meet all applicable state standards. 4) A VDOT land use permit will be required for any work within the VDOT right of way and may be obtained at the VDOT Harrisonburg residency office. Should the safety, use, or maintenance level of any existing or proposed entrance to a VDOT maintained highway change in the future, VDOT reserves the right to require additional modifications as warranted by the site-specific conditions. Staff recommends that we make requirements from VDOT a condition of the SUP. Health Department- Per Jeffery Mason with the Page County Health Department, “No health department issues w/ request. Note: Certification letters could be potentially Null/Void if drainfield areas are disturbed.” Staff recommends that we make requirements from the Health Department a condition of the SUP. Building Official- Per James Campbell, Page County Building Official, “No objection to request. Applicable permits will be required prior to construction.” Staff recommends that we make the requirements from the Building Official a condition of the SUP. PAGE COUNTY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is located in the “Agricultural Protection Tier.” Per the Comprehensive Plan, the purpose of the Agricultural Protection Tier is “[t]o protect (to keep from being damaged or lost) agricultural uses and preserve the rural lifestyle and sense of community that has long defined Page County” (Volume 1-9). Further, the Comprehensive Plan states the following: “This tier is intended primarily for very low-density residential development, large lot rural development and agricultural uses. Non-residential uses would serve the needs of residents in the surrounding rural areas and generally be limited to agriculture-related businesses.” (Volume 1-23, 24). Policies within the Comprehensive Plan (Volume I, Chapter 3) include (other policies may also be relevant): • Goal 2, Policy 2.1: “Preserve a rural lifestyle in the County outside of the towns, Incorporated Areas Tier and Community Service Area Tiers.” (Volume 1-66). • Goal 3, Policy 3.2: “Preserve and protect agricultural uses and the rural lifestyle and sense of community that has long defined Page County, especially in the Agricultural Protection Tier.” (Volume 1-68). • Goal 3, Policy 3.16: “Minimize conflicts between agriculture and non-agricultural land uses. (Volume 1-70). • Goal 6, Policy 6.2: “Encourage economic growth that is compatible with the County's rural character while generating a positive net cash flow for the County” (Volume 1-74). • Goal 6, Policy 6.9: “Encourage commercial and industrial business to locate in industrial parks and existing commercial centers or designated growth areas” (Volume 1-74). • Goal 6, Policy 6.10: “Allow commercial and industrial uses in rural areas or near existing neighborhoods only if the use: a. Does not unduly impede traffic flow on roads or intersections; b. Is not, and does not, initiate strip development; c. Has direct access to adequate roads, railroads or airports; d. Meets all standards for water, sewage and waste disposal; and e. Does not adversely affect surrounding agricultural or residential activities” (Volume 1-74). Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is a portion of a larger lot that was divided via 25-acre divisions and non-family divisions, along with a boundary line adjustment, in 2024, as well as court-authorized divisions in 2025. The only residential address located within approximately 500 ft. of Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is 2844 US HWY 340, located on the west side of US HWY 340. 2845 US HWY 340 is the physical address for a poultry structure located approximately 50 ft. from the southwest parcel line of 59-(A)-63F. 2195 US HWY 340 is the address for structures previously operated as Page Valley Flea Market, located within a Commercial (C-1) split-zoned portion of Tax Map 59-(A)-40. This split-zoned portion of lot 59-A-40 is approximately 60 ft. from one corner of Tax Map 59-A-63F. Tax Map 59-(A)-63F does not have access to public water or wastewater. Contained within in the application packet is the applicant’s “Comprehensive Plan Compliance Narrative,” which includes a table of policies and consistency analysis of most of the policies listed, above. Planning staff generally concurs with the conclusions represented, here, including the assertion that the Zoning Ordinance reflects “the County’s own determination that a facility of this type can coexist with the district’s agricultural purpose without altering the land’s underlying agricultural zoning or availability for future agriculture use.” Staff notes that “rural character” may be interpreted in different ways. The Comprehensive Plan provides a general framework in Exhibit 5: Development Guidelines; however, a commercial storage land use does not necessarily fit cleanly within the “Rural Business” category. The Zoning Ordinance’s allowance of this use in the Agriculture zoning district by special use permit suggests that Rural Business may be a comparable “Land Use Type” from Exhibit 5. Staff recommends the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors consider appropriate conditions to address potential adverse impact of this use brought forward during the public hearing(s). MOTION(S): I move that the Page County Planning Commission recommend approval of the special use permit to operate a self-storage facility with the attached conditions on property located off US Hwy 340, Stanley, VA, and further identified by tax map number 59-(A)-63F. OR I move that the Page County Planning Commission recommend denial of the special use permit to operate a self-storage facility with the attached conditions on property located off US Hwy 340, Stanley, VA, and further identified by tax map number 59-(A)-63F. OR I move an alternative motion. No email should ever ask you for your username or password.] Good evening Sandy and Ken, I am a resident of District 4 and am reaching out regarding two related issues on the agenda for tomorrow's meeting. Item A in the Unfinished Business section, the Special Use Permit for Flowerdew Hundred LLC, is a concerning proposal. This property is one parcel away from our family farm so while I am not one of the neighbors who must be notified of the SUP, I am certainly in the "neighborhood". I disagree with the permit application on a number of fronts. First and foremost, this property is in the Agricultural Protection Tier and while I understand the land will still be zoned agricultural, a self storage facility is certainly not an agricultural use. There is nothing similar in this part of the county. Even the neighboring property that is split-zoned commercial, is a pair of old chicken houses that can be used for commercial purposes. Seven self storage buildings will certainly change the character of this area. Additionally, I would argue that there really isn't a shortage of self storage available in the county. There are 9 self storage facilities within 10 miles of this site. I called and checked on-line at several facilities last week and all had multiple units available. The SUP application references a precedent of other storage unit facilities that were created by SUP on agriculturally zoned parcels, but I notice that all the existing storage facilities are located very near the town borders. None are so far out in the county as this proposal. Additionally, the proposal as submitted will have limited economic benefit and does not provide any permanent employment. Lastly, the proposed development will generate a new source of light pollution and the increase in impervious surface will certainly impact Hawksclaw Creek right before it joins with the South Fork. I do not think this proposal is a wise use of land in our Agricultural Protection Tier. This brings me the larger issue that you all will discuss tomorrow, Item B in the Unfinished Business section, the Subdivision of Land Discussion. Specifically, the concept of 25-acre subdivisions. While I appreciate the efforts to tighten down on 25 acre divisions, requiring a 5year wait period before another division, I encourage the Planning Commission to consider fully removing the 25-acre division clause from the subdivision ordinance. According to the Census of Agriculture, Page County lost more farmland between 2017 and 2022 than any neighboring county - 20%. All the while, citizens and elected officials have made it clear that protecting farmland is a priority. How can we say it's a priority while we allow so much farmland to be converted to other uses? One way we could act is to completely remove the 25 acre exception for subdivision. These divisions eat up our remaining farmland and allow for what are ultimately unplanned residential subdivision far from amenities, jobs, and services and/or special use permits for incompatible commercial enterprises, like self storage facilities, in rural areas. Removing the 25 acre exception is not anti-growth, it is in fact protecting the land base for our largest economic asset - agriculture. I urge the Planning Commission to remove the 25 acre exception from the subdivision ordinance entirely. Powers 3834 Old Buckingham Road Mark A Kinney, Vice-Chair Powhatan, Virginia 23139 County Administrator William Hagy Barbara Brown The County of Powhatan HONORING THE POWHATAN COUNTY VOLUNTEER RESCUE SQUAD ON THE OCCASION OF ITS 70TH ANNIVERSARY OF SERVICE WHEREAS, the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad was established in 1956 by dedicated citizens who recognized the importance of providing emergency medical care and rescue services to their neighbors and fellow citizens; and WHEREAS, for seventy years, the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad has faithfully served the residents and visitors of Powhatan County, Virginia, answering calls for assistance, responding to emergencies, and providing compassionate care during times of greatest need; and WHEREAS, throughout its seven decades of service, the Squad has demonstrated an unwavering commitment to preserving life, protecting the health and safety of the community, and providing emergency medical and rescue services with professionalism, dedication, and compassion; and WHEREAS, the success and continued strength of the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad are a testament to the countless volunteers, career personnel, officers, leadership, auxiliary members, and supporters who have generously contributed their time, talents, and resources in service to others; and WHEREAS, the members of the Squad have answered the call to serve regardless of the hour, the weather, or the circumstances, often placing the needs of others before their own and exemplifying the very best traditions of volunteerism, selflessness, and community service; and WHEREAS, the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad has played an essential role in the public safety system of Powhatan County, working in partnership with fellow emergency services personnel, public safety agencies, healthcare providers, and community organizations to safeguard the well-being of our citizens; and WHEREAS, the 70th anniversary of the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad provides an opportunity for the Board of Supervisors and the entire community to recognize and express sincere appreciation for seven decades of extraordinary commitment, sacrifice, and service, 4 P-2026-22 while honoring the legacy of those who came before and celebrating those who continue this vital mission today. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED, that the Powhatan County Board of Supervisors, on behalf of the citizens of Powhatan County, Virginia, hereby recognizes and celebrates the 70th Anniversary of the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad, honoring its seventy years of dedicated service to the Community of Powhatan County. BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED, that the Board of Supervisors extends its deepest gratitude and appreciation to all past and present members, volunteers, leadership, and supporters of the Powhatan County Volunteer Rescue Squad for their unwavering dedication, courage, compassion, and commitment to the health, safety, and well-being of our community. BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED, that the Board of Supervisors encourages all citizens of Powhatan County to join in recognizing this significant milestone and celebrating the legacy of service established in 1956 and carried forward through generations of dedicated rescue squad members. Water/Wastewater Master Plan Review Page 1 of 7 11 POWHATAN COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS WORKSHOP MINUTES OCTOBER 8, 2026 Mr. Hagy reminded the Board of the details of the 2025 water and wastewater master plan. He cited business growth in the Dutoy Creek service area as straining sewer capacity, and said the choice is between halting new connections and an intermediate solution. If the Board agrees with the direction, light engineering would follow to inform FY28 CIP cost estimates. Mr. Kinney and Mr. Hagy discussed utilization of the sewer area. Mr. Powers asked what level of analysis the engineering funding in FY28 would cover. Mr. Hagy said the ideal sewer buildout has each business connect to a public pump station, but businesses have built private pump stations connecting directly to the force main. Mr. Kinney stated constituents will question why this issue wasn’t addressed by past boards. Mr. Hagy discussed how prior funding and infrastructure decisions contributed to the current constraints Mr. Powers asked about the timeline for building a pump station. Mr. Glidewell responded it takes about three years. Mr. Kinney asked if it would be feasible to add another business at this time. Mr. Hagy said 22 private pump stations are now connected to the force main in the Dutoy Creek service area. He said this puts the utilities department in a difficult position. Mr. Kinney said the county cannot rebalance tax revenue without adding new businesses, and it lacks the infrastructure to do so. Mr. Hagy said staff had an intermediate proposal. He displayed the Route 60 growth area and showed that connecting new projects the old way would compound the existing problem. In response to a question about a specific property, Mr. Glidewell said the business proposed building its own private pump station and maintaining it themselves since the owner had security concerns about county access to the site. Page 2 of 7 12 POWHATAN COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS WORKSHOP MINUTES OCTOBER 8, 2026 Mr. Kinney asked whether developers of recently rezoned properties could put businesses on them without issue. Mr. Glidewell said private pump stations at those sites could be built to switch to gravity sewers once a public pump station exists. He said the casings under Route 60 were placed with future pump stations in mind, but nothing was ever connected. Mr. Hagy said staff is developing a two-part solution. Mr. Kinney asked whether the businesses would have to pay for it. Mr. Glidewell said there is little price difference between a progressive cavity pump and a centrifugal pump. He said the discussion would center on a smaller public pump station that businesses could connect to. Mr. Powers asked if the pump stations are modular. Mr. Glidewell said he doesn't believe so, but a smaller station’s tanks could be made bigger in the future. Charla Schubert, Finance Director, discussed the pre-audit fund balance and expected reserves for FY27. Mr. Kinney calculated what remains of the fund balance after that 15% is removed. He asked whether the county could pay for the interim solution from fund balance rather than debt. Mrs. Schubert explained $8.9 million remains in the capital maintenance reserve after current CIP commitments. She said funding this project from it is possible but would drain the reserve. Mr. Hagy said staff could look at moving faster than the FY28 CIP, possibly by funding only engineering and design. He said the one pump station is programmed for FY33 because debt affordability in the early years is limited and committed to other projects. He said the A&E and construction were planned for the same year. He said A&E could take six to nine months, so construction could start within that same year. text: 1 2 3 4 Attachment 1 The Smyth County Board of Supervisors held its regular meeting on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. The location of the meeting was in the First-Floor Board Room of the County Office Building, 121 Bagley Circle, Suite 100, Marion, Virginia. PRESENT: Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins Chilhowie District Supervisor Mike Sturgill North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call ABSENT: None STAFF: County Administrator Shawn Utt Asst. County Administrator – Operations, Lisa Richardson Asst. County Administrator – Development, Clegg Williams Zoning Administrator Becca Creasy County Attorney Andrew McBride OTHERS: Smyth News & Messenger and approximately 20 citizens 10/22/2026 5:00 PM Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins called the meeting to order and welcomed everyone. 10/22/2026 5:00 PM County Administrator, Shawn Utt, led the pledge of allegiance. Jessica Davidson led the invocation. 10/22/2026 5:03 PM County Administrator Shawn Utt requested the Board amend the agenda to add Citizen’s Time and Sheriff’s Office Shooting Range update. After discussion, the following motion was made:  Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener made a motion to amend the agenda to add Citizen’s Time and an update to the Smyth County Sheriff’s Office shooting range. Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill seconded the motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:05 PM County Administrator Shawn Utt read the rules for public hearings. 10/22/2026 5:05 PM Charles Hayden of Marion shared his opinion about a potential conflict of interest involving a county employee’s connection with the Town of Marion’s EDA as a Board member. 10/22/2026 5:07 PM Joe Naff of Countryside Drive in Marion criticized the ordinance regarding data centers, stating that it was poorly written. He questioned whether the matter would need to go to court and requested that the Board repeal the ordinance to allow additional public input and reconsideration, with the Board voting again in front of its constituents. 10/22/2026 5:09 PM David Fulton of Marion expressed concerns that the process related to the data center ordinance had lacked transparency, questioning why a developer seeking to develop property would not want public support. He suggested that the lack of openness raised concerns about whether information was being withheld from the public. 10/22/2026 5:10 PM Charles Wassum of Wassona Drive in Marion expressed appreciation for the return of the Citizens’ Time item to the Board’s agenda. 10/22/2026 5:11 PM Judy Wyant of Marion questioned the transparency surrounding the data center text amendment and whether revenue was the primary motivation. She challenged Board members to face their constituents and answer for their decisions. She expressed offense at being directed to the County’s website for information, accused Board members of slander, and requested a public apology. She encouraged citizens to continue speaking up and reminded Board members of their accountability to the public. 10/22/2026 5:14 PM With no other citizens wishing to speak, Chairman, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins closed citizen’s time 10/22/2026 5:14 PM With no presentations, Chairman, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins moved on to the adoption of October 5, 2026, and October 8, 2026, meeting’s minutes: After further discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris to approve October 5, 2026, minutes as amended. Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. After further discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call to approve October 8, 2026, minutes as presented. Royal Oak District Supervisor Rick Billings seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:16 PM Budget Discussion and Update – County Administrator Shawn Utt reported that the draft budget still reflected an additional $539,628 in cuts to be resolved through further discussions with the Smyth County School System which could result in the schools losing additional state funding as well. Board members discussed the proposed reduction in school funding, the County’s rising expenses compared to revenue, and whether additional cuts could be identified without reducing school funding. Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill cautioned that reducing the local match could affect school programs like preschool and clarified that the decisions regarding program cuts would be made by the School Board. The discussion also addressed the potential impact of reducing DSS funding on future state funding. Several members emphasized the importance of doing everything possible to avoid cuts that would negatively affect children. 10/22/2026 5:31 PM County Administrator, Shawn Utt, proposed an additional work session focused on identifying approximately $540,000 in further budget cuts elsewhere in the budget if the Board wanted to minimize impacts on schools. The Board discussed holding a special-called meeting on November 5, 2026, at 5:00 p.m., to address the remaining cuts and finalize the budget. After further discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Royal Oak District Supervisor Rick Billings to hold a special-called meeting on November 5, 2026, at 5 p.m. to address the remaining cuts and finalize the budget. Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:42 PM Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins entertained a motion to approve the following November Appropriation requests: - General County Operations: EDA (Fund 004): Smyth County Schools (Fund 009): Smyth County DSS (Fund 013): $ $ $ $ 2,768,937.00 700,000.00 5,790,000.00 697,898.00 - OAA Grant Funds (Fund 240): OAA Direct Distribution (Fund 241) E-Summons (Fund 748): Total Appropriation Requests: $ $ $ $ 2,946,528.00 86,090.00 2,000.00 12,991,453.00 After discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call to approve the November Appropriation Requests as presented. Vice-Chairman Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:43 PM Chairman, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins entertained a motion to approve the Transfer Requests. 1. Dennis Greer, Superintendent of Buildings and Grounds, requested the following transfers: a. $6,000 transfer from Health Department Maintenance Contracts (001-43030-3005) to Administration Building Maintenance Contracts (001-43040-3005) to cover unanticipated costs associated with the Trane maintenance contract. b. $2,000 transfer from Health Department Repair & Maintenance Supplies (001-430305407) to Library Maintenance (001-73010-5407) for additional maintenance work at the Library. After discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener to approve the Transfer Requests as presented. Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:48 PM Chairman, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins entertained a motion to pay the second half of October invoices and additional $275K for CSA costs as presented. After discussion, the following motion was made:  Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener made a motion to approve paying the 2 nd half of October invoices in addition to the CSA accounts payable as presented. Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris seconded the motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: None. ABSENT: None. 10/22/2026 5:54 PM Future Board Work Session Locations Discussion – County Administrator Shawn Utt discussed plans to establish a portable meeting setup to allow Board meetings to be held throughout the County. The Board discussed selecting meeting locations during regular meetings, with consideration given to holding joint public hearings with the Planning Commission in the affected districts. Members suggested identifying two to three suitable locations. Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener supported holding meetings throughout the County, particularly for special use permit matters, and emphasized that Planning Commission scheduling should not prevent this effort. Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris requested that the IT Department evaluate and approve potential locations in advance. The Board also discussed the possibility of prioritizing video recording over livestreaming, with recordings posted online after meetings. County Administrator Shawn Utt confirmed that the changes were expected to take effect in January. Members emphasized the importance of ensuring the public was aware of meeting locations and had equal opportunities to attend. 10/22/2026 6:05 PM Morison Building (County Administration Building) Improvements Discussion – Assistant County Administrator Clegg Williams discussed the need to evaluate critical building systems at the Morison Building, noting that relocating County offices was not financially feasible in the near future but approximately $3 million remains in the Building Improvements bond. SMYTH COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION Thursday, October 22, 2026 The Smyth County Planning Commission met in their regular meeting on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at 6:30 P.M. in the Smyth County Office Building. Commissioners Present: Hazel Wagoner, Chairperson, Atkins District; Graham Davidson Jr., Vice-Chairman, Chilhowie District; David C. Buchanan Jr., Saltville District; Robert Campbell, North Fork District; Tony Dean, Royal Oak District; Lea Meadows, Park District; and Paul Shepherd, Rye Valley District Staff Present: Clegg Williams, Becca Creasy, Jessica Davidson, and Kelsey Marchant Adoption of Agenda: Hazel Wagoner called the meeting to order. David Buchanan Jr. made a motion to adopt the agenda as presented. It was seconded by Graham Davidson Jr. and followed by a unanimous vote. Minutes: Lea Meadows made a motion to approve the minutes as presented of the Thursday, August 27, 2026, meeting. It was seconded by Mr. Buchanan Jr. and unanimously approved. Amendment to June 25, 2026, Meeting Minutes: Ms. Meadows made a motion to amend the meeting minutes for June 25, 2026, to include Charles Wassum’s name on the speaker’s list. It was seconded by Mr. Buchanan Jr. and unanimously approved. Citizens’ Time: At 6:33 PM, Dr. Charles Wassum thanked the Commissioners for adding his name to the June 25 minutes, but did not understand why he was left out, considering the newspapers mentioned him. Mr. Buchanan Jr. interjected that people do make mistakes. Dr. Wassum continued with his speaking time, going over the purposes of zoning; the future land use map; what was allowed by right and by special use permit; and that the comprehensive plan’s zoning map should be the official zoning map. He also reiterated his sentiments that data centers should not be allowed by right or special use permit in the agricultural and agricultural/rural districts. He ended his speaking time stating that he filed a complaint with the circuit court concerning the Board accepting the Planning Commission’s recommendation of the data centers text amendment. Update from the Zoning Administrator: Clegg Williams indicated that considering the recent text amendment, he thought it appropriate to update the comprehensive plan. He suggested incorporating overlay districts, where data centers are built within one mile of AEP high voltage lines. He asked the Commissioners if that would be something they would be interested in considering; they agreed. Dr. Wassum stated that that would be considered an update to the comprehensive plan, which needs to be updated every five years. Questions/Comments from Commissioners: Mr. Davidson Jr. asked if we could update the by-laws to include substitutes on the ordinance committee, for when a commissioner could not make it to a committee meeting. Mr. Williams said that we could review the by-laws in January. Recess: At 6:45 PM, Mrs. Wagoner recessed the meeting for a joint public hearing with the Board of Supervisors. The Smyth County Comprehensive Plan does not identify a density range, and the general usage of the property has been farmland. The property is located beside 6066 Lee Hwy in Atkins, Virginia, and is identified as Tax Map Nos. 49B-1-18 through 49B-1-24. 2) A special use permit application from Laurel Creek Energy Storage II LLC to establish a Battery Storage Facility on Maloyed Place behind the AEP Substation at 3456 Saltville Hwy in Saltville, Virginia, further identified as being Tax Map No. 18-1-9 and zoned Agricultural/Rural. Any person may appear and be heard on this matter, subject to the rules of the Smyth County Board of Supervisors and Planning Commission. Application materials are available for public review in the offices of the Zoning Administrator and County Administrator, 121 Bagley Circle, Marion, Virginia, during regular business hours. Persons requiring special assistance under the Americans with Disabilities Act should contact (276) 706-8315 at least 48 hours prior to the hearing. Smyth County complies with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act; for information call (276) 783-3298 or visit www.smythcounty.org. Done by order of the Board of Supervisors and the Planning Commission. Shawn Utt, County Administrator Hazel Wagoner, Chairperson of the Planning Commission 10/22/2026 7:10 PM Shawn Utt read the rules of the public hearing into the record and then turned it over to Mr. Williams. Mr. Williams introduced Ella Roberts, who applied for map amendment to rezone her property from Commercial to Agricultural/Rural. 10/22/2026 7:12 PM Mrs. Roberts informed the Board and Commissioners that her and her husband had lived on the adjoining property for nearly thirty years and recently bought the property next door and were unsure what to do with it. They finally decided they wanted to build their home on the property and wanted to get it rezoned. 10/22/2026 7:13 PM Charles Atkins asked for a rough idea of where they were planning on placing their home on the property and what they were going to do with the barn already located at the site. Mrs. Roberts said that they had planned on building their home towards the center of the property and that they would keep the barn on the site. 10/22/2026 7:14 PM There were no further questions from the Board and the Commissioners. Jeff West of Crowe Hollow Road was the only person who signed up to speak. He said that he was on the Human Rights Committee in Richmond and said that the Roberts had a right to use their property how they wanted to and that the Board and Commissioners should let her use it however she intended. 10/22/2026 7:16 PM With no further comments, Mr. Williams introduced the special use permit application for Laurel Creek Energy Storage Facility II. He then explained that the Board approved the first special use permit for Laurel Creek Energy in 2023, with thirty conditions He then turned it over to Rex Young, the representative for Laurel Creek. 10/22/2026 7:18 PM Mr. Young reintroduced himself to the Board and the Commissioners, as he represented the first storage facility. He then proceeded with a Power Point presentation describing his company’s goals for the property, what a battery storage facility is, and what the benefits would be of approving another facility. 10/22/2026 7:30 PM Robert Campbell asked why they’ve taken so long for the previous battery storage facility to be built. Mr. Young indicated that they were at the mercy of Pennsylvania-Maryland-Jersey (PMJ), the primary grid operator, which has been a long process, and that they are doing their environmental study and waiting on approval from the State Corporation Commission. PC Meeting Minutes October 22, 2026 Page 3 David Buchanan Jr. took note of the 2028 deadline on the previous special use permit and wondered if he had any information on when they could begin building. Mr. Young stated that he hoped to have more information in January. Mr. Buchanan then asked if they would meet the renewal deadline of 2032 for the second special use permit application. Mr. Young said that he is aware of the renewal, and that he hopes it will be online by then. 10/22/2026 7:33 PM Mike Sturgill asked how many megawatts the proposed facility was, what the benefit was for the citizens, and asked for a plain explanation of what a battery storage facility is. Mr. Young indicated that this facility would be 375 megawatts, while the first approved facility was 250. Mr. Young explained that a battery storage facility made sure electricity was not wasted. Essentially, the battery absorbs extra electricity that is not being used and will discharge it during peak hours of electricity usage. Hopefully, this will help with electricity costs and be able to get power re-established during storms. 10/22/2026 7:35 PM Jason Parris asked if the batteries were a self-contained unit and about their safety concerns. Mr. Young stated that they had many safety features and that they go by the latest fire code to help meet those standards. He stated that they have a full life-cycle plan for the structure, with an early life safety plan drafted. He also said they would provide life safety training and will partner with fire safety coordinators. He then added that the facility would be monitored 24/7. In terms of safety, Ms. Meadows asked what the risk of fire would be during a surge. Mr. Young stated that they were currently doing a study. 10/22/2026 7:43 PM Mr. Atkins asked how long battery storage function could provide electricity, once it was up and running. Mr. Young stated that it would be a four-hour period. He stated that they wanted electricity to be available during peak usage and when there was the most stress to the energy system. 10/22/2026 7:47 PM Mr. Buchanan applauded how thorough the decommissioning plan was for the facility. Roscoe Call then had questions about the property, if it were ever to be decommissioned. Mr. Young stated that the land would not be contaminated and could be used again, if decommissioned. Mr. Call then expressed concerns about the property being purchased by a foreign country. Mr. Young stated that the only people who would own it would be Laurel Creek. He also stated that they were regulated in those regards, having cyber security. 10/22/2026 7:51 PM Mr. Parris took note of the 20-year goals and asked if they would continue to make those long-term goals. Mr. Young said that was the hope, with them only having to change out batteries. 10/22/2026 7:52 PM With no further questions from the Board and the Commissioners, there was only one person from the community who signed up to speak. Mr. Jeff West of Crowe Hollow Road asked questions about lithium disposal; why not offer a battery to members of the community and not waste land; what the half-life was of a battery; and who would replace them. He stated that there were no geologists present to answer questions and that, overall, the batteries were not good for the environment. 10/22/2026 7:56 PM Mr. Atkins asked if there were any more people who wanted to speak. Mr. Glenn Moore of Johnston Road asked who makes the decision of where power goes to and when. Both Mr. Young and Mr. Williams stated that it goes back to the grid. Mr. Young then stated that the distribution system then flows through Smyth County or elsewhere. 10/22/2026 7:58 PM Dr. Charles Wassum, Wassona Drive, then spoke, asking about how much power Plus Power provides to electrical companies. Mr. Young indicated that once power was on the grid, it didn’t necessarily have to be Appalachian Power, and that they did not have any control of who the customer was. 10/22/2026 8:00 PM Mr. Parris asked one more question concerning battery life. He asked if a battery had to be replaced, if that would be on Laurel Creek Energy Storage. Mr. Young indicated that it was warrantied, insured, and bonded through them. Mr. Campbell then asked if that included disposal; Mr. Young confirmed. A citizen then asked what would happen if the company went bankrupt. Mr. Young stated that everything would be bonded through their insurance company, and that he had to show evidence of it. 10/22/2026 8:02 PM With no further questions or comments, Mr. Atkins adjourned the joint public hearing. 10/22/2026 8:05 PM Mrs. Wagoner reconvened the Planning Commission. She asked if there were any comments from the Commissioners concerning the map amendment. With none, she asked for a motion. PC Meeting Minutes October 22, 2026 Page 4 10/22/2026 8:06 PM Donald & Ella Roberts – Map Amendment (Tax Map Nos. 49B-1-18 through 49B-1-23): Tony Dean made a motion to recommend the Board of Supervisors approve the Map Amendment to rezone parcels beside 6066 Lee Highway, Atkins from Commercial (C) to Agricultural/Rural (A/R). Ms. Meadows seconded the motion, and the following vote was recorded: Vote: 7 yeas 0 nays Buchanan Jr., Campbell, Davidson Jr., Dean, Meadows, Shepherd, and Wagoner 10/22/2026 8:07 PM Mrs. Wagoner asked if there were any comments concerning the special use permit application. With none, she asked for a motion. 10/22/2026 8:09 PM Laurel Creek Energy Storage Facility II – Battery Storage Facility Special Use Permit (Tax Map No. 18-1-9): David Buchanan Jr. made a motion to recommend the Board of Supervisors approve the Special Use Permit for a battery storage facility located at Maloyed Place in Saltville, with the same 30 conditions, with the exception that the five-year expiration date be extended to six years. title: Packet
text: TOWN OF SOUTH BOSTON REGULAR MEETING MINUTES TUESDAY OCTOBER 13, 2026 y gee ie ON COUNCIL CHAMBERS 420 MAIN STREET SOUTH BOSTON, VA 24592 CALL TO ORDER AND INVOCATION Mayor Edward Owens called to order a regular South Boston Town Council meeting at 7:00 pm on October 13, 2026. ROLL CALL Present: Mayor Edward Owens, Vice-Mayor Sharon Harris, Councilman Joe Chandler, Councilman Tommy Elliott, Councilwoman Barbara Speece, Councilman Brian Burton, Councilwoman Tina Younger Absent: Also Present: Town Manager Matthew Candland, Town Clerk Sarah Lowe, Finance Director Danyell Duncan, Public Works Director John Hatcher, Police Chief Ronnie Edmonds, Fire Chief Ray Conner, Recreation Director Matthew McCargo APPROVAL OF MINUTES On motion of Councilwoman Speece, seconded by Councilman Chandler the meeting minutes from the Town Council’s regular meeting on September 14, 2026, were approved. APPROVAL OF THE CONSENT AGENDA On motion of Councilwoman Younger, seconded by Vice-Mayor Harris, the agenda for October 13, 2026 was approved following moving item number five the resolution supporting the dog park financial match to number six and moving the Harris Park Pavilion to item number five. AGENDA 63 | Page 1. RESOLUTION IN HONOR OF VIRGINIA “POO” ROBERTS Councilman Tommy Elliott stated that it was an honor to read a resolution in memory of his dear friend, Virginia “Poo” Roberts. Before reading the resolution, Councilman Elliott shared personal remarks about Mrs. Roberts; anyone who had never met Mrs. Roberts had missed a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, and described her as having it all: looks, style, personality, and wit. Mrs. Roberts had been his ninth-grade English teacher, chauffeur to freshman away basketball games, and, most of all, a dear friend. Councilman Elliott said that calling her unique was an understatement. She was kind and considerate, and she could also be firm and demanding when needed, which her son Christian could likely confirm. He noted that Mrs. Roberts was very prominent in South Boston and Halifax County and will be missed by all. In closing, Councilman Elliott said, “Poo, I know you’re listening, because you did not miss much. We love you and we miss you, but most of all, we’re thankful you were a part of our lives. Rest in peace, dear.” Councilman Elliott then read the following resolution: WHEREAS, Virginia “Poo” Roberts devoted a lifetime of service to the Town of South Boston and Halifax County as an educator, civic leader, and tireless volunteer; and WHEREAS, Mrs. Roberts taught English at Halifax County High School and championed education throughout her life, serving on the Danville Community College Advisory Board and the Danville Community College Educational Foundation; and WHEREAS, through her leadership with the South Boston Industrial Development Authority, Mrs. Roberts helped attract physicians and industries to the area, developed residential subdivisions, strengthened downtown businesses, and was instrumental in bringing the YMCA and Commonwealth Assisted Living to South Boston; and WHEREAS, Mrs. Roberts gave generously of her time to the Bloodmobile, the United Way, the Halifax Community Hospital Auxiliary, the South Boston Garden Club, and the Master Gardener Program; and WHEREAS, her vision, generosity, and leadership have left a lasting imprint on the Town that will benefit its citizens for generations to come; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Town Council of the Town of South Boston, Virginia, honors the memory of Virginia Ann Hunt Roberts and expresses its deep gratitude for her dedicated service to this community; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this resolution be spread upon the minutes of the Town Council and a copy be presented to her family as an expression of the Town's respect and appreciation. Adopted this 13th day of October, 2026. 2. YARD WASTE ORDINANCE Patrick Elwell, Assistant Manager, stated that this item was continued from the previous month’s meeting, where several questions had come up about the penalty section of the 64|Page ordinance. Background information addressing those questions was included in the agenda packet. Mr. Elwell explained that the proposed ordinance is unchanged from the version presented at the last meeting. The penalty section was adopted in February, and the proposed amendment makes no changes to it. Council could amend the proposed ordinance to change the penalty section if it wished. However, staff recommended keeping the current language and offered to answer any questions about the penalty section. On motion of Councilman Burton, seconded by Councilman Chandler, Council approved the yard waste ordinance. . MUTUAL AID AGREEMENT WITH HALIFAX COUNTY Chief Ronnie Edmonds presented the mutual aid agreement between the South Boston Police Department, the Halifax County Sheriff's Office, and the Town of Halifax Police Department. Chief Edmonds explained that under the agreement, the agencies assist one another when additional help is needed on a call. As examples, he cited the recent shooting on North Main Street and the incident on Seymour Drive, when assisting agencies provided extra personnel to help secure the scenes. The South Boston Police Department provides the same assistance to the other agencies when they request it. Councilwoman Speece commented that it is great that the three agencies cooperate and work together so well. Chief Edmonds agreed, adding that the agreement provides more manpower to secure scenes. On motion of Councilwoman Speece, seconded by Vice-Mayor Harris, Council approved the mutual aid agreement with Halifax County by voice vote. . TRANSFER OF HOWERTON COURT Assistant Town Manager, Patrick Elwell reported that Earl Howerton of Poplar Creek Homes, LLC has proposed donating Howerton Court, currently a private roadway, to the Town. If accepted, the Town would become responsible for its maintenance and repairs. Staff confirmed that the road is understood to meet VDOT specifications. Staff also noted that the road was not cleared during last year’s ice event because it is not part of the Town system. Council discussed the long-term financial impact of maintaining the roadway and asked who originally paid for its construction. Staff will research that question. By consensus, Council directed staff to proceed with the transfer process. Staff will return with a formal deed or plat revision, along with the financial impacts, for Council’s approval. . HARRIS PARK PAVILION Mr. Elwell continued last month’s discussion of park capital improvement projects. Staff explained that a pavilion had been planned for Harris Park, but the funds allocated for the project were not enough to build it. The question came up in connection with the Riverdale Dog Park discussion, and Council was asked whether it wanted to make the pavilion its next park capital improvement project. On motion of Councilman Burton seconded by Councilwoman Younger, Council voted by voice vote to make the Harris Park Pavilion the Town’s next capital improvement project. 65|Page 6. RESOLUTION SUPPORTING THE PROPOSED DOG PARK FINANCIAL MATCH Mr. Elwell continued last month’s discussion of the proposed dog park presented by Ryland Clark. Under the proposal, the community would raise up to $100,000, and the Town would contribute matching funds. The project is estimated to cost about $150,000. The resolution would accept the $100,000 raised by the community and pledge up to $75,000 from the Town to complete the project, with the community funds coming first. Christian Roberts reported that the group has received $25,550 in pledges from nine contributors so far. A design has been completed, with separate areas for large and small dogs and a water station. Usage rules have not yet been developed. Mr. Elwell noted that additional work, including FEMA verification, will be needed before construction. Town support would also help the group pursue matching grants. On motion of Councilman Elliott, seconded by Councilwoman Speece, Council approved the resolution supporting the dog park financial match by the following vote: Voting aye: Elliott, Speece, Burton, Harris, Chandler; Voting nay: Younger; Absent and not voting: None. 7. SIDEWALKS ON NORTH MAIN STREET Assistant Manager, Patrick Elwell continued the earlier discussion of residents’ requests for sidewalks along North Main Street, from the new Dominion building to the Wendy’s property on Old Halifax Road. Staff explained that the project would require VDOT review, identifying funding sources, and acquiring right-of-way from about 35 property owners, either by donation or, if necessary, through eminent domain. Staff gave a very rough preliminary estimate of $2 to $3 million under ideal conditions, and noted that final costs would likely be higher. Staff would seek VDOT funding to cover most or all of the project, and an engineering firm may be needed for preliminary design. Council asked staff to bring an estimate of engineering costs to the next meeting. Staff noted that the remaining timeline depends on VDOT. Staff has not yet contacted property owners along the corridor, and that would be one of the first steps. Staff also explained that North Main Street extends to Dan River Church Road, but the sidewalk would need to continue to Wendy’s to connect with existing sidewalks and a crosswalk. It was noted that many pedestrians walk in the street and ditches along the corridor, making this a safety issue. By consensus, Council directed staff to proceed with contacting VDOT and property owners and to report back with preliminary information. 8. FOOD TRUCK DISCUSSION Patrick Elwell reported that a food truck operator recently asked to set up on a Town-owned parking lot. Staff found that the Town Code says very little about food trucks outside of permitted and downtown events. Staff recommended drafting an amendment to the Town Code to set out food truck regulations, including a formal permit process, and asked for Council’s consensus and any guidance on where and under what conditions food trucks should be allowed to operate. Councilwoman Speece asked that any regulations be practical 66|Page and enforceable, citing the lessons learned from the yard waste ordinance. In response to Council’s questions, staff said the ordinance would apply to stationary food trucks. Staff would also consider whether ice cream and snow cone trucks should be included and would define “food truck” in the code. Noise from vendor trucks would continue to be governed by the Town’s noise ordinance. Staff confirmed that the current code allows a food truck to stay in one location for three days, and the Zoning Administrator may extend that by up to seven additional days. Staff confirmed the Town can enforce this limit. Staff was asked to look into any problems with collecting meals tax from food trucks and to close any loopholes. Also, to consider a designated food truck park or regular food truck days. That would give local vendors a place to set up within Town limits and keep that revenue in the community. By consensus, Council directed staff to draft a proposed food truck ordinance for Council’s review. 9. INTRODUCTION OF ASMITA POUDEL Patrick Elwell introduced Asmita Poudel, the Town’s new Community Standards Specialist. Mrs. Poudel holds degrees in architecture, urban and regional planning, and organizational leadership. She is a member of the American Institute of Certified Planners and most recently worked as a planning specialist for the City of Seattle. She is beginning arapid assessment of the Town’s housing stock, which will guide future code enforcement efforts. Mrs. Poudel thanked Council and said she looks forward to serving the community. Council welcomed her. 10.FINANCE REPORT Danyell Duncan presented the financial report through August 31, 2026, two months into the fiscal year. The General Fund collected $1,759,369.46 in revenue and spent $2,057,476.36, for a net position of $298,106.90. She noted that this is normal for this time of year, because real estate and personal property taxes are not due until later. Revenue highlights included: cigarette tax, $17,234; occupancy tax, $57,210; telecommunications tax, $57,388; utility tax, $62,900; bank stock tax, $93,004.93, a prior-year payment received late; local sales tax, $118,786; and meals tax, $461,121. The 2026 real estate and personal property tax bills have been mailed, and early payments have been strong. Department spending ranged from 6% to 20% of budget. Capital spending to date has gone mainly to the fire department and Town Hall building renovations. Several annual expenses, including dues, debt service, and contracts, were paid early in the year. Major revenues such as loan proceeds, grant funding, and reimbursements have not yet been received. These timing differences are expected and will be monitored throughout the year. There were no questions from Council. 11. TOWN MANAGER UPDATES Patrick Elwell, Assistant Town Manager gave several updates. The Harris Park ribbon cutting is scheduled for Saturday, November 14, at 2:00 p.m., with afternoon and evening events planned. At Vaughan Street Park, the old tennis court fencing has been removed, 67 |Page and a contractor will resurface the courts in spring 2027. The courts will have one full tennis court, one full pickleball court, and a pickleball court inlaid in the tennis court. In response to a question from about the drop-off at the courts, staff stated that new fencing will be installed along the same perimeter after resurfacing. The historic district expansion is progressing: Hill Studio surveyed properties in the expanded district last week, and the project is expected to be completed in summer 2027. The South Boston Cruise-In will be held Sunday, October 18, from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m. downtown. Destination Downtown South Boston was one of 110 organizations selected for a $50,000 Downtown Investment Grant, which will expand the Main Street flower project throughout downtown. Councilwoman Speece congratulated Destination Downtown South Boston, noting that visitors often compliment the downtown’s appearance. In response to a question from Mayor Owens, staff reported that the Main Street housing project is complete except for the CDBG grant closeout paperwork, and the project sign will be removed once closeout is finished. 12.CITIZEN COMMENTS Brian Brown, 1502 Irish Street, Director of the Halifax County Industrial Development Authority, reported that the IDA has closed on the purchase of the Greens Folly Golf Course for a mixed-use housing development. The project will focus on workforce housing for households earning up to 150% of the area median income, about $115,000 or less for a family of four. It will come before Council as a planned unit development at an estimated five to six units per acre, below the ten units per acre the ordinance allows. Mr. Brown invited Council to contact the IDA with any questions or concerns. Anthony Womack, a Town Planning Commission member and longtime youth mentor, thanked Council for improvements to the playground and the temporary sidewalk. He described community events held at the playground this year, including Prayer at the Playground, an Easter egg hunt, and a kickball tournament. He also described a teacher appreciation day at the elementary school held in partnership with Dollar General. He noted that the upcoming event will coincide with the Harris Park ribbon cutting. He thanked Council for prioritizing the park project ahead of the dog park and noted some concerns about the second phase. Another resident thanked the Town for its grass cutting and roadway maintenance. The resident asked the Town to improve trash and debris removal in areas near downtown. This resident also supported prioritizing the parks and asked for more activities for families with young children. It was also noted for the Town to make the community more walkable, including sidewalks in the Glendale area or extending the Tobacco Heritage Trail. Council asked staff to look at sight distance problems at the intersection of Webster and Portland Street. Joe Acree, Town Fire Official, addressed food truck regulations. He explained that under the fire code, food trucks that cook with grease must be permitted. He can permit only vehicles based in the Town, and trucks from other localities or states must be permitted in their home jurisdiction before operating here. Trucks must be set back at least ten feet from vehicles, buildings, and combustible materials. He noted that he works with Tamyra Vest, Destination Downtown to make sure food trucks at Town events are permitted ahead 68 | Page
